en: The Scripture on the Samādhi of Gathering All Merit, Scroll One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at the Great Dharma Garden of Āmra trees in Vaiśālī.
In the lecture hall, he was together with a great assembly of ten thousand bhikṣus—all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions;
whose minds had attained mastery, whose minds had attained excellent liberation, and whose wisdom had attained excellent liberation; whose minds were as disciplined and supple as great dragon kings;

who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, achieved their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, and reached the other shore. He was also accompanied by twenty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive, had attained dhāraṇīs and unimpeded eloquence, possessed great supernormal powers, were well-able to give rise to various profound samādhis, and—through firm vows of mindfulness and wisdom, and through wisdom and skillful means—had reached the other shore. Their names were as follows:

The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas Cāritramati, Siṃhamati, Varṇamati, Vardhamānamati, Vardhanamati, Amitamati, Dharmamati, Maitreya bodhisattva-mahāsattva, Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta bodhisattva-mahāsattva, and Nārāyaṇa bodhisattva-mahāsattva—these were the leaders among twenty thousand bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there were forty thousand devaputras—all of whom were oriented toward the Mahāyāna—as well as countless other Śakras, Brahmās, and Lokapālas.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis who paid him reverent homage, and he preached the Dharma for them.
At that time, the World-Honored One was to relinquish his physical life and enter parinirvāṇa in three months.
At that moment, the Buddha-dharma was supreme and wondrous, flourishing to such an extent that it eclipsed all the various non-Buddhist paths.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa, Lord of a thousand worlds, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The Tathāgata will before long relinquish his body and life, entering ultimate parinirvāṇa.
Now, the Dharma of the Tathāgata is the most supreme; it can completely eclipse all those outside the path who lack faith and reverence.
“Excellent, World-Honored One!

We only pray that the Tathāgata will protect all bodhisattvas, enabling them to manifest all manner of goodness in this present life, causing their roots of goodness to increase, their minds to be joyful, and their majestic virtue to flourish; may they never sever the lineage of the Buddhas, and may they uphold the Eye of the Dharma and the Eye of the Saṃgha.”
I only pray that the Tathāgata will gather in and rescue all sentient beings, and distinguishingly expound the path toward Nirvāṇa.

May the True Dharma thus taught, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, be circulated by all Bodhisattvas without interruption, and may Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi long abide in the world, so that they may never be separated from seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dharma, and making offerings to the Saṅgha.

He increases the power of mindfulness so as not to forget any dharmas; he increases the power of wisdom to awaken to and understand profound dharmas; he increases the power of diligence to attain progress and the understanding of meanings; he possesses the power of shame (*hrī*) to purify his own mind; he possesses the power of remorse (*apatrāpya*) to abandon all unwholesome dharmas; he attains the power of firmness because his deportment is complete; he possesses the strength of robust vigor to sever and eliminate all fetters (*saṃyojana*); and he possesses the great heroism of fearlessness in whatever he dwells.
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva not lose their merit, not lose the true Dharma, not lose wisdom, not lose knowledge, and not lose the bodhicitta; how do they possess firm resolve and mindfulness, reach the ultimate in spiritual friendship, lead all sentient beings even unto nirvāṇa, act according to their words, and abide in the fulfillment of the Buddha-dharmas without deceiving sentient beings?”

Without seeking anything for oneself, they relinquish everything; abiding according to the teachings, they dwell in the three pure precepts; abiding in pure patience themselves, their minds are free from coarseness and ferocity; toward all sentient beings, their minds are impartial; abiding in diligence themselves, they perform all deeds; abiding in the various dhyānas themselves, they possess the three wholesome precepts; well-abiding in loving-kindness themselves, they do not rely on or cling to any meditative concentrations; abiding in clear wisdom themselves, they are free from all false views and attain illumination regarding all phenomena; using the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather in sentient beings without weariness, they do not seek gratitude or recompense;
they constantly mindfully practice all that constitutes the wholesome realms of humans and devas, and they abide in the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) like a threshold.

The mind does not incline toward the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; the mind always inclines toward the Dharma and does not incline toward desire. It seeks the benefit of the Dharma King rather than the benefit of humans or devas; it practices wisdom and acts according to what is taught by the Buddha’s wisdom. It sustains its life through the Dharma rather than living on food and drink; it remains far removed from greed while embracing all beings, far removed from anger with no intent to harm any sentient being, and far removed from delusion, thereby leaving behind the darkness of all dharmas. Having transcended all Māras and being free from all fetters and afflictions, one skillfully employs expedient means to properly enter all gateways.
When he had asked this,
the World-Honored One then addressed Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of a thousand worlds:
“Excellent!”
Excellent,
Nārāyaṇa! It is well that you are now able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such a matter for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
Nārāyaṇa! Listen now attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall explain to you these various practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the merit obtained from which exceeds even this.
Then the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa, filled with joy, addressed the Buddha, saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
Having received the instruction, he listened.
The Buddha told Nārāyaṇa:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have a samādhi called ‘Gathering All Meritorious Virtues.’”

When a bodhisattva accomplishes this samādhi, they do not lose their merit, do not lose the true Dharma, do not lose wisdom, do not lose knowledge, and do not lose the opportunity to see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and make offerings to the Saṃgha; they diligently practice the four means of attraction, abide personally in giving, and so on, up to abiding personally in skillful means, thereby accomplishing these virtues as well as other merits.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had expounded and proclaimed the name of this Samādhi of the Accumulation of All Merit, he remained silent.
Then, there was a great strongman named Viśuddhatejas, who possessed great strength and resided in the great city of Vaiśālī. He thought to himself:
"I am a great strongman endowed with great strength; among all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, there is none whose strength equals mine."
"I have previously heard that the śramaṇa Gautama has attained great power and possesses the body of Nārāyaṇa endowed with the ten powers.
He further thought to himself:
"I shall go to see whether the śramaṇa Gautama is my equal or not."
At that time, the Malla Śuddhānanda departed from the great city of Vaiśālī and proceeded toward the Great Dharma Lecture Hall in the Āmra Garden.

Having arrived, he beheld the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; the Buddha’s great majesty was such that a multitude of hundreds of thousands surrounded him with reverence as he expounded the Dharma. He appeared like Mount Sumeru rising from the great ocean, majestic on all sides and exceedingly sublime.

When he first beheld the Tathāgata, he attained a heart of great faith, joy, love, and reverence; he immediately prostrated himself on the ground, paid homage at the feet of the Tathāgata, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then withdrew to stand to one side with palms joined above his head, contemplating the Buddha with single-minded focus.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the mind of the Māṇavaka Śuddhasthāma and wishing to subdue him, addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Maudgalyāyana!
Go and fetch the arrow I used long ago when I was a bodhisattva, during the contest of strength for the sake of winning Gopī, the daughter of the Śākya clan."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana said to the World-Honored One,
"I do not see or know where he is. Thereupon,

the World-Honored One emitted from his right foot a great radiance called "Illumination," and this light shone everywhere throughout this Buddha-world of the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system.
At that time, beneath this trichiliocosm, a great adamantine wheel-arrow stood upright there.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Do you see this great adamantine wheel-arrow standing upright there in this world-system?"
Maudgalyāyana replied:
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana, “Go and bring it here.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana descended to that place; as quickly as a strong man might bend and extend his arm, the entire great assembly saw him depart. He then brought it back and presented it to the Tathāgata, speaking these words:
“World-Honored One!
Is this the power born of his parents when he was a bodhisattva?
Or is it the power of supernormal faculties?”
The Buddha said:
"This was the power born of his parents when he was a bodhisattva, not the power of supernatural faculties (ṛddhi),
Maudgalyāyana!"
"If a Bodhisattva were to employ the power of supernatural penetrations, this arrow would pass beyond immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds.
The Venerable Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"This is indeed the power of the merit born of the parents of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"The strength of ten men is equal to the strength of one robust ox; the strength of ten robust oxen is equal to the strength of one blue ox."
Ten of the strength of a blue ox equal the strength of one ordinary elephant; ten of the strength of an ordinary elephant equal the strength of one *roca* elephant;
ten of the strength of a *roca* elephant equal the strength of one *kani* elephant; ten of the strength of a *kani* elephant equal the strength of one fragrant elephant (*gandhahastin*);

ten of the strength of a fragrant elephant equal the strength of one *vidha* elephant; ten of the strength of a *vidha* elephant... [ten of the strength of a *vidha* elephant equal the strength of one *mahāvidha* elephant].
The strength of ten ordinary fighting elephants is equal to the strength of one non-fighting elephant; the strength of ten non-fighting elephants is equal to the strength of one *īṣādhara* elephant;
the strength of ten *īṣādhara* elephants is equal to the strength of one *praśānta* elephant; the strength of ten *praśānta* elephants is equal to the strength of one *bhadra* elephant;
the strength of ten *bhadra* elephants is equal to the strength of one blue elephant; [the strength of ten blue elephants is equal to the strength of one... *nīla* elephant.
The strength of ten ordinary yellow elephants is equal to the strength of one red elephant; the strength of ten red elephants is equal to the strength of one white elephant;
the strength of ten white elephants is equal to the strength of one red lotus elephant;
the strength of ten red lotus elephants is equal to the strength of one pink lotus elephant; and ten pink lotus elephants are equal to [the strength of one great elephant].
The strength of one gandhahastin is equal to ten gandhahastins; the strength of ten great gandhahastins is equal to the strength of one lion-king bound by a snare;
the strength of ten lion-kings bound by a snare is equal to the strength of one strongman;
the strength of ten strongmen is equal to the strength of one mahābala; the strength of ten mahābalas is equal to...
One *cāṇūra* strength; ten *cāṇūra* strengths equal one great *cāṇūra* strength; ten great *cāṇūra* strengths equal one *pāñcajanya* strength;
ten *pāñcajanya* strengths equal one great *pāñcajanya* strength; ten great *pāñcajanya* strengths equal the strength of a terrestrial deity (*bhūmideva*);
ten [terrestrial deities]... [equal the strength of a] *bhūmideva*... [and so on].

The power of one *devaputra* of the Hall of Heaven is equal to the power of ten *devaputras* of the Hall of Heaven; the power of ten *devaputras* of the Hall of Heaven is equal to the power of one *devaputra* of the Wind-Sustaining Heaven (*Vāyu-dhara-deva*);
the power of ten *devaputras* of the Wind-Sustaining Heaven is equal to the power of one *devaputra* of the Garland-Sustaining Heaven (*Mālā-dhara-deva*);

the power of ten *devaputras* of the Garland-Sustaining Heaven is equal to the power of one *devaputra* of the Ever-Intoxicated Heaven (*Sadāmada-deva*); and the power of ten *devaputras* of the Ever-Intoxicated Heaven is equal to the power of one *devaputra* among the Four Great Kings (*Catur-mahārāja-kāyika*).
The strength of all the sons of gods among the Four Great Kings is equal to the strength of one king of those gods;

the strength of ten kings of those gods is equal to the strength of one son of the gods among the Thirty-three Gods; the strength of all the sons of gods among the Thirty-three Gods is equal to the strength of one Śakra;
the strength of ten Śakras is equal to the strength of one son of the gods among the Yāma Heaven. One...
The power of all the sons of gods in the Suyāma Heaven is equal to the power of one Suyāma Heavenly King;

the power of ten Suyāma Heavenly Kings is equal to the power of one son of a god in the Tuṣita Heaven; the power of all the sons of gods in the Tuṣita Heaven is equal to the power of one Tuṣita Heavenly King;
and the power of ten Tuṣita Heavenly Kings is equal to [the power of] one Nirmāṇarati Heavenly King.
The power of one son of heaven among the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*) is equal to the power of all the sons of heaven in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations;

the power of ten such kings of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations is equal to the power of one son of heaven among the gods of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*);
the power of all the sons of heaven in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations is equal to the power of one [son of heaven] in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations.
The power of ten kings is equal to the power of one son of the gods among the Paranirmita-vaśavartin deities;
the power of all the sons of the gods among the Māra heavens is equal to the power of one Māra king; the power of ten Māra kings is equal to half the power of Nārāyaṇa;
the power of ten half-Nārāyaṇas is equal to the power of one Nārāyaṇa; ten [Nārāyaṇas]...
The strength of one Mahānārāyaṇa is equal to the strength of ten Nārāyaṇas; the strength of ten Mahānārāyaṇas is equal to the strength of a bodhisattva who has practiced for one hundred kalpas;
the strength of a bodhisattva who has practiced for one hundred kalpas is equal to the strength of a bodhisattva who has practiced for one thousand kalpas;
the strength of a bodhisattva who has practiced for ten thousand kalpas is equal to the strength of a bodhisattva who has practiced for ten thousand kalpas.
The power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for one hundred thousand kalpas is equal to the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for ten hundred thousand kalpas;
the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for ten hundred thousand kalpas is equal to the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for one million kalpas;
the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for one million kalpas is equal to the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for ten million kalpas.
The power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for ten million kalpas is equal to the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for one hundred million kalpas;
the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for one hundred million kalpas is equal to the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for one billion kalpas;
the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for one billion kalpas is equal to the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for ten billion kalpas.

The power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for ten thousand kalpas; the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for one hundred, one thousand, ten thousand, and one hundred million kalpas; equal to the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for one billion kalpas;
equal to the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for ten billion kalpas; equal to the power of a bodhisattva who has practiced for one hundred billion kalpas; ten trillion... [and so on].
The power of a Bodhisattva who has practiced for a thousand million *kalpas* is equal to the power of ten thousand thousand million *kalpas* of practicing Bodhisattvas;

the power of a Bodhisattva who has practiced for one hundred thousand thousand million *kalpas* is equal to the power of a single Bodhisattva who has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
and the power of ten such Bodhisattvas who have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas is equal to the power of a single Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
The power of ten bodhisattvas of the tenth stage is equal to the power of one bodhisattva in his final birth.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana,
because the bodhisattva has accomplished such power, he was able to walk seven steps immediately upon birth.
“Maudgalyāyana!
If the Buddha did not sustain this world, it would perish and fail to remain. Why is this?
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has been born and takes his seven steps, this world-system’s great earth extends sixty-eight thousand yojanas in breadth;
as soon as the Bodhisattva has been born and places his foot down, it immediately sinks down by one hundred thousand yojanas;
when he lifts his foot again, it rises up once more by one hundred thousand yojanas.
By virtue of the Buddha’s sustaining power, this world remains unmoved and unimpaired, and sentient beings are free from affliction.
At the very moment a bodhisattva in their final birth is first conceived, they already possess such power.
“Maudgalyāyana!
The power of ten newly born bodhisattvas is equal to the power of one bodhisattva in the prime of life.
Maudgalyāyana!”
The bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes this power and proceeds toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to awaken to bodhi;
when thus proceeding toward the site of enlightenment, this power exceeds that of the power possessed while seated at the site of enlightenment by a hundred thousandfold.
Furthermore, having accomplished and perfected such immeasurable, boundless, asaṃkhyeya, unobtainable, and indestructible power, he eventually attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“Maudgalyāyana!

Suppose all sentient beings in every world were to attain the power of a bodhisattva who is fully endowed and on the verge of achieving enlightenment; compared to the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), it would not equal even one part in hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, or millions of billions, nor could it be reached by any calculation or analogy.”
Having attained these ten kinds of powers, one is named Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, the power of the Tathāgata is sustained by fundamental roots of goodness; it neither increases nor decreases.

In this context, the supernormal powers of the bodhisattva are not explicitly explained; however, if a bodhisattva were to employ such powers, they could place worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges upon a single hair-tip at the end of a toe and cast them beyond immeasurable and boundless worlds, as many as the sands of the Ganges.
Thus coming and going, he does not cause sentient beings to experience suffering or affliction;
such spiritual power is immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, unfathomable, incalculable, and unequaled.
If the Tathāgata were to manifest all his supernatural powers, even you śrāvakas would be unable to believe them, let alone other sentient beings.
“Maudgalyāyana!

When a bodhisattva proceeds to the site of enlightenment, he contemplates that the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element are all a single realm, namely, the realm of space.”
"Therefore, the great earth is not destroyed, and sentient beings suffer no affliction.
At that time, the Malla Śuddhasthāman, having heard from the Tathāgata this discourse on the power born of the parents of a bodhisattva, [was filled with joy].
Having heard this, he was struck with wonder and amazement such that the hairs on his body stood on end;
he conceived a sense of rare and marvelous faith. Rising from his seat, he adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have now completely crushed all my pride, having heard from the Tathāgata concerning the powers of a bodhisattva.
World-Honored One!

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, and I resolve to attain the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, desiring to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, and vowing to fully realize the power of the Tathāgata.
At that time, ten thousand devaputras, having heard the words spoken by the Malla Śuddhasthāman, all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, and they also thought:
“World-Honored One!...”
"May we obtain such power as that of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is now present.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is called the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of the Accumulation of All Merit?
Having first spoken these words, the Tathāgata remained silent."
“World-Honored One!
We now pray that you will expound and explain this Samādhi of the Accumulation of All Merit; how does a bodhisattva attain this samādhi?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa, Lord of a Thousand Worlds:
"Nārāyaṇa! There is no bodhisattva who has resolved upon the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment who does not follow this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit."
Why is this? Nārāyaṇa,
there are no meritorious virtues that do not enter into the mind of one who has first resolved upon enlightenment.
Just as all rivers and streams have no flow that does not enter the great ocean, so it is, Nārāyaṇa!

All merit—whether derived from giving, ethical discipline, or cultivation; whether with outflows or without outflows; mundane or supramundane; whether pertaining to gods or humans—is entirely encompassed within the mind set upon awakening (bodhicitta).
Therefore, Nārāyaṇa!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to accumulate all merits and virtues, they should resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path of enlightenment.

"Nārāyaṇa! It is like the jewel mountains—namely Sumeru, Meru, Mahāmeru, Cakravāḍa, and Mahācakravāḍa—as well as all other mountains, medicinal herbs, trees, and forests; villages, towns, and large and small cities; Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Aparagoyānī, and Uttarakuru—the four continents; as well as the thousand-world system, the two-thousand-world system, and the three-thousand great thousand-world system; the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; and the sun, moon, and stars, including their eclipses—all these are contained within the three-thousand great thousand-world system, even up to ten billion sets of four continents, all of which are situated therein."
Thus it is, Nārāyaṇa!

All the merit of all ordinary beings, the merit of those in training (śaikṣa), the merit of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), the merit of bodhisattvas, and the merit of Tathāgatas—all are subsumed within the initial resolve of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, Nārāyaṇa!
If you wish to encompass all merit, you should resolve to attain the unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment of a bodhisattva.

"Nārāyaṇa! If all sentient beings in the four continents were each endowed with the merit of a universal wheel-turning monarch, the merit and wisdom of one who has first resolved to attain the Mahāyāna path would still be far superior to theirs."

Nārāyaṇa! Suppose all sentient beings in the four continents, even all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm who are included within the realm of sentient beings—each and every one of these sentient beings were to possess the merit of a universal wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin rāja). Let the merit of all these wheel-turning monarchs constitute a single mass of merit for one wheel-turning monarch, and let each and every sentient being again possess that same amount of merit.
"What do you think?
Would these merits not be very great? Nārāyaṇa said:
“If the merit of this single person is already immeasurably vast, how much more so the accumulation of virtue belonging to immeasurable asaṃkhyeya people?
The Buddha said, “Nārāyaṇa!”

Setting aside all sentient beings in this trichiliocosm, even if all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were each to possess the merit of a great universal wheel-turning king.
Nārāyaṇa! What do you think?
Is this accumulation of virtues not indeed great?
Nārāyaṇa said:
“World-Honored One!

Even if all sentient beings in a single trichiliocosm were to possess the full accumulation of virtues of a universal wheel-turning monarch, they would still be immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable in number.”
"How much more so for the beings in immeasurable and boundless worlds who possess the full accumulation of merit of a great wheel-turning king? "Nārāyaṇa!

Now that I have understood this, I declare: compared to the accumulation of merit belonging to one who has first resolved upon bodhicitta, all previous accumulations of merit do not equal even a hundredth part; they do not equal a thousandth, a hundred-thousandth, a hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor can they be reached by any calculation or analogy."
"Nārāyaṇa! This is called the first teaching on entering the Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa!"
Nārāyaṇa! Suppose the Brahmā King of a thousandfold world-system possesses a heart of loving-kindness that universally pervades this entire thousandfold world-system;
and suppose there were another person who were to give as a gift the seven treasures filling that same thousandfold world-system.
"What do you think?
Between the merit of this person’s giving and the merit of Brahmā’s compassion, which is superior?
Nārāyaṇa replied:
“World-Honored One!
The Brahma King’s merit from loving-kindness is immeasurable and boundless. “Nārāyaṇa!”
Setting aside the compassionate mind of the Brahmā King of this thousandfold world system, Nārāyaṇa!
Suppose the compassionate mind of the Brahmā King of a two-thousandfold world system were to pervade and completely fill this two-thousandfold world system.
Furthermore, suppose there were someone who took seven treasures filling two thousand worlds and used them to practice giving. What do you think?
Between the merit of this person’s giving and the merit of the Brahma King’s compassion, which is superior?
Nārāyaṇa said:
“World-Honored One!
The compassionate merit of the Brahmā King is immeasurable and boundless.”

"Nārāyaṇa! Suppose the Brahmā King of this trichiliocosm were to fill this entire trichiliocosm with a mind of universal loving-kindness; and suppose, furthermore, that someone were to give as a gift the seven treasures filling this entire trichiliocosm."
"What do you think?
Between the merit of this person’s giving and the merit of Brahmā’s loving-kindness, which is superior?
Nārāyaṇa replied:
“World-Honored One!
The compassionate merit of the Brahma King is immeasurable and boundless. Nārāyaṇa said:
“World-Honored One!

The merit of giving does not equal even one hundredth part of the merit of loving-kindness; it does not equal one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation, analogy, or metaphor.”
The Buddha said:

"In this way, Nārāyaṇa, the Brahmā king of four thousand worlds has a mind of loving-kindness that also pervades these four thousand worlds; the Brahmā king of five thousand worlds has a mind of loving-kindness that also pervades these five thousand worlds; the Brahmā king of ten thousand worlds has a mind of loving-kindness that also pervades these ten thousand worlds; and the Brahmā king of a hundred thousand worlds has a mind of loving-kindness that also pervades these hundred thousand worlds."

If a person were to take all the seven treasures filling hundreds of thousands of worlds and offer them as a gift, the mass of merit thereby obtained would be surpassed by the merit of loving-kindness; the merit of loving-kindness is superior.

"Nārāyaṇa! Suppose all sentient beings within these three thousand great thousandfold worlds were each to possess a mind of loving-kindness equal to the mind of loving-kindness possessed by the Great Brahmā King of a hundred thousand worlds—the aggregate of merit from all such minds of loving-kindness [would be as follows]."

If one were to compare this to a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind on enlightenment, whose aspiration is focused and superior, who acts without illusion or deceit for the sake of liberating all sentient beings, and who truly cultivates the merit of a compassionate heart for the sake of all beings—the former would not equal even one hundredth part of the latter; it would not equal one thousandth, one hundred-thousandth, one hundred-millionth, one ten-billionth, or one trillionth part, nor could it be reached by any calculation or analogy.
"Nārāyaṇa! Therefore, you should know that if one wishes to cultivate and accumulate all merits, this son or daughter of good family should resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Those who have now set forth and those who shall set forth in the future will be fully endowed with such an immeasurable and boundless accumulation of merit; this is the second teaching on entering the Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
"Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa!
What do you think?
Is the space in the eastern direction pervasive?"
"Are all the empty spaces in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below universally pervaded?
Nārāyaṇa replied:
"World-Honored One!"
“Even the eastern void cannot have its limits found, let alone the unspeakably immeasurable and boundless void that pervades all worlds throughout the ten directions.
The Buddha said, “Nārāyaṇa!”

Suppose there were a person who, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, were to employ various analogies and explanations, desiring to reach the limits of empty space; yet they would never find those limits.

Nārāyaṇa! I shall now employ a parable to clarify this meaning, desiring to bring to full completion this Samādhi that Collects All Merit, and also to increase the resolve of those sentient beings who cultivate and accumulate merit, and to cause the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the Mahāyāna to fulfill their great diligence.

"Nārāyaṇa! Suppose one were to fill the trichiliocosm with mustard seeds, even up to the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, filling it completely with mustard seeds. Even if someone were to carry them across worlds as numerous as the sands of a hundred thousand Ganges Rivers toward the east, dropping a single mustard seed at each step, and continuing thus toward the east until all those seeds were exhausted, they still could not reach the limit of the world-systems;
the same would apply to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir."
Nārāyaṇa! Suppose there were worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, filled to the brim with mustard seeds. Nārāyaṇa!
Is there any among gods or humans who could count all these mustard seeds and know their number?
Then Nārāyaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all sentient beings in the four continents were to achieve wisdom equal to that of Śāriputra, they would still be unable to count even a single fraction of it within the span of an eon, let alone be able to exhaustively count a great heap of mustard seeds.”

"Nārāyaṇa! Suppose someone were to place a single mustard seed beyond as many worlds in the eastern direction as there are sands in the Ganges River; proceeding thus eastward until all those mustard seeds were exhausted, one would still not reach the limit of those worlds.
It is the same for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir."
Nārāyaṇa! Thus, this world is pervaded by empty space; suppose there were humans and devas who filled it with the seven kinds of precious jewels and offered them as a gift. Nārāyaṇa!
"What do you think?
Would this mass of merit not be great?
Nārāyaṇa replied:
“Immeasurable, World-Honored One!
Boundless, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"Nārāyaṇa! If one were to compare the mass of merit possessed by such a person with the mass of merit accumulated by a bodhisattva who has first resolved for enlightenment—one who has accomplished their aspiration, is free from illusion and deceit, practices with diligent vigor, and gives rise to great loving-kindness and great compassion for the sake of liberating all sentient beings—the former’s gift of merit does not equal even a hundredth part of the latter; it cannot even be approached by calculation or analogy."
Nārāyaṇa! All things and all space throughout the ten directions are completely pervaded. Nārāyaṇa!
The compassionate mind of a bodhisattva is likewise; it fills the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions and universally encompasses all sentient beings.

"Nārāyaṇa! To all those sentient beings reached by this Bodhisattva’s mind of loving-kindness, he causes them to be fully endowed with all the merit possessed by a great Wheel-Turning King, as well as all the merit possessed by Śakra, and all the merit possessed by Brahmā."

If there is a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon the mind of enlightenment, who is single-mindedly intent on its realization, free from illusion and deceit, and who practices with diligent vigor; who, for the sake of liberating all sentient beings, gives rise to a heart of compassion and directs themselves toward that goal—the merit obtained through such compassionate action surpasses the merit acquired by all those sentient beings who possess the status of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), Śakra, or Brahmā.
Nārāyaṇa! This is the third teaching on entering the Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
"Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa!"

Even if all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to possess the merit of a universal wheel-turning monarch, it would not equal even one hundredth part of the merit of Śakra; indeed, it would be beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.

Nārāyaṇa! Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were each to become Śakra; their combined merit would not equal even one hundredth of that possessed by a Brahmā King, nor could it even be reached through calculation, analogy, or comparison.

"Nārāyaṇa! Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were each to possess the merit and wisdom of a Great Brahmā Deva King; compared to the merit and wisdom of a single lay follower (upāsaka) who has severed desire, their combined amount would not equal even one hundredth part of his, nor could it even be reached by calculation."

Nārāyaṇa! Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were to possess the merit and wisdom of an upāsaka who has severed desire; compared to the merit and wisdom possessed by Śāriputra, their portion would not equal even one hundredth part, nor could it be reached even by calculation or analogy.

"Nārāyaṇa! Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm possessed merit and wisdom equal to that of Śāriputra; compared to the merit and wisdom of a single pratyekabuddha, they would not equal even one hundredth part, nor could they be reached by any calculation or analogy."

Nārāyaṇa! If all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm were to possess all the merit and wisdom of a pratyekabuddha, they would not equal even one hundredth part of the merit and wisdom possessed by a single bodhisattva who has practiced for five hundred kalpas.
"One should train in this way to enter the Samādhi of the Accumulation of All Merit.
When this Dharma was spoken, thirty-two thousand sentient beings all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
This trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the music of humans and devas played simultaneously; humans and devas rained down flowers that accumulated up to the knees.
The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors all spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
These who have first resolved their minds for enlightenment are all superior to us."
World-Honored One!
We, too, shall benefit these good men and good women who have already generated, are now generating, or will in the future generate the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

As we understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if there are sentient beings who do not resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, they will be unable to approach this Samādhi that Accumulates All Merit, nor can they enter it correctly;

if there are sentient beings who do resolve to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, they will be able to approach this Samādhi that Accumulates All Merit, and they will also be able to enter it correctly.
At that time, the Malla Śuddhasthāman addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what dharma can one achieve the accomplishment of this Samādhi that Gathers All Merit?”
The Buddha said: "Good son,
by accomplishing one dharma, you will encompass this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit."
What is this one dharma?
It is not abandoning the mind of omniscience.
Son of good family!
This is called accomplishing one dharma that encompasses this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
Furthermore, son of good family,
there are again two dharmas that encompass this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit;
That is to say: never being weary of hearing the Dharma, and practicing it after having heard it.
Son of good family!
These are called the two dharmas that accomplish the inclusion of this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
"Furthermore, noble son,
one further accomplishes three dharmas that encompass this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
What are these three?
That is to say: abandoning all evils, practicing wholesome dharmas, and skillfully dedicating [the merit].
Son of good family!
These are called the three dharmas that accomplish this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
"Furthermore, good son, there are four further dharmas that encompass this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit;
namely: purity of precepts, purity of view, purity of mind, and purity of wisdom."
"Noble son!
These are called the four dharmas that accomplish and encompass this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
Furthermore, noble son!"
Furthermore, one accomplishes five dharmas that encompass this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
What are these five? They are:

focusing the mind to resolve upon bodhicitta; always speaking truthful words; being free from flattery and deceit; being free from envy; and maintaining a mind that is always equal toward all sentient beings.
“Good son! These are called the five dharmas that accomplish and encompass this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
Furthermore, good son!”
Furthermore, one accomplishes six dharmas that encompass this Samādhi of the Accumulation of All Merit.
What are these six? They are:

drawing near to spiritual friends, distancing oneself from evil associates, staying far away from the clamor of crowds, dwelling in quiet seclusion, not abandoning great loving-kindness, and giving rise to great compassion for all sentient beings.
"Good son!
These are called the six dharmas that accomplish this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
Furthermore, good son!"
Furthermore, one accomplishes seven dharmas that encompass this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.

What are these seven? They are: practicing meditative concentration; being skilled in wisdom; being skilled in knowing causes; being skilled in knowing conditions; abiding in uprightness; cultivating and gathering the Path; and being without indolence while practicing the Path.
"Good son!
These are called the seven dharmas that accomplish this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
Furthermore, good son!"
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas that encompass this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
What are these eight? They are:

flexibility of body, flexibility of mind, contemplation of feelings, contemplation of phenomena; ensuring that unarisen evil dharmas do not arise, severing and extinguishing evil dharmas that have already arisen, employing skillful means to give rise to unarisen wholesome dharmas, and protecting and increasing wholesome dharmas that have already arisen.
“Good son!
These are called the eight dharmas that accomplish this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
Furthermore, good son!”
Furthermore, there are nine dharmas that accomplish this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
What are the nine? They are:

contemplating the inexhaustibility of past phenomena, the inexhaustibility of present phenomena, and the inexhaustibility of future phenomena; contemplating phenomena as being like illusions; awakening equally to the three periods of time; knowing all phenomena as they are and accepting them with patience; not slandering emptiness; not discriminating regarding signlessness; and not aspiring toward any form of existence.
"Noble son!
These are called the nine dharmas that accomplish this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
Furthermore, noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas that encompass this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
What are these ten? They are: understanding selflessness;

enduring the absence of a life-principle; not doubting the absence of a person; taking conditioned phenomena as impermanent; regarding all places of birth as being like a hell; viewing the four great elements as poisonous snakes; viewing the sense bases as an empty village; viewing the aggregates as executioners; eliminating all notions of existence; and delighting in the cultivation of liberation.
“Good son!
These are called the ten dharmas that accomplish this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.
At that time, the Malla Virūpakṣa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to accomplish all adornments of merit, they should listen to this samādhi;
if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to gather all merit, they should listen to this samādhi.”
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain inconceivable merit, they should believe in this samādhi and listen to this samādhi;
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to attain inexhaustible merit, they should practice this samādhi;
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to reach the great ocean of all merit, they should receive, uphold, read, recite, cultivate, and explain this samādhi.
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to attain the marks of the hundred merits, they should practice this samādhi.
At that time, the Malla Vimala again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

With what dharmas is a bodhisattva mahāsattva associated and endowed so as to fulfill all these adornments of merit, to cultivate and accumulate all merit, inconceivable merit, inexhaustible merit, and the ocean-like merit that fulfills the marks of a hundred blessings?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Malla Śuddhatejas: "Good son!

There are three dharmas that serve as pillars of merit, adornments of merit, the gathering of merit, the expansion of merit, the inexhaustibility of merit, the great ocean of merit, and the inconceivability of merit."
What are the three? They are:
first, the adornment of generosity; second, the adornment of ethical discipline; and third, the adornment of extensive learning. "Good son!
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice the adornment of giving?
Son of good family!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should give rise to this thought: when practicing giving, one does not perceive the mind of giving, nor does one perceive the object given or the recipient, nor does one perceive one's retinue.

If there are beggars who come with requests, for the sake of gathering and protecting them, he does not harbor stinginess or give rise to a contrary mind regarding his royal throne, fiefdoms, wealth, or various precious treasures.
“Good son! This bodhisattva mahāsattva forms this thought:
‘Now I have already bestowed this very body of mine upon all sentient beings; how much more so other material wealth?’”
If I have already given, I shall never harbor a mind of regret. Should anyone require wealth, I shall give wealth;

should they require food, I shall give food; should they require drink, I shall give drink; should they require eyes, I shall give eyes; should they require flesh, I shall give flesh; should they require blood, I shall give blood; should they require marrow, I shall give marrow; should they require limbs and joints, I shall give limbs and joints; should they require a head, I shall give my head—I shall give all these, let alone other material possessions.

There is nothing I do not give away—be it rice, gold and silver, clothing, necklaces, elephants and horses, carriages, cities and kingdoms, royal palaces, men and women, wives and concubines, servants, or retinues. If there are sentient beings who seek whatever they require, I shall give them everything I possess without any anxiety or regret, and without looking for any reward.
"Arising a mind of compassion to gather in sentient beings, one continues to gather them until the attainment of Buddhahood, never coming to an end.
"Good son! If there is a bodhisattva who gives rise to such a mind, it is called the adornment of a bodhisattva’s giving."
"Furthermore, good son!
A bodhisattva does not regard or calculate his own body or life; he would rather sacrifice his body and life than ever commit evil.
He does not maintain himself through wrong livelihood for the sake of nourishing the body; he would rather sacrifice his body and life than cause affliction to others."

They do not commit various evils for the sake of fiefs or estates; they do not engage in fierce disputes for the sake of their kin; nor, for the sake of wives, concubines, sons, or daughters, do they envy the wealth of others, nor give rise to avarice. They are always and ever few in desire, never giving rise to even a single thought of an evil mind, let alone many.

To sever stinginess and greed, one does not give rise to anger; because there is no anger, one accords with right practice; because one accords with right practice, one reaches the right state; because one reaches the right state, one accords with right precepts; because one accords with right precepts, one associates with virtuous friends and reverently makes offerings to them; because one reverently makes offerings to virtuous friends, one hears the true Dharma; having heard the true Dharma, one practices according to what was taught; having practiced according to what was taught, one is then able to benefit sentient beings on false paths, refrains from all evils, and accords with wholesome dharmas; thus one comes to know skillful means and knows the faculties of sentient beings.
"Good son! It is because this bodhisattva adorns his practice of giving that he attains these merits.
Furthermore, good son!"

A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not give rise to the notion of internal or external regarding either the internal earth element or the external earth element; they regard them as equal and without distinction. Why is this?

The body is like a wall, a tree, or grass; it is like a shadow, like a mirage; it is without cognition, without thought, without volition, and without solidity, being comprised of the four great elements.
If there are those who cut or hack them with knives and staves, or strike them with tiles and stones, they never give rise to retaliation.

They do not regard or calculate their own bodies, nor do they cherish their own lives; they harbor no anger toward sentient beings, for they have cultivated a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all.
“Good son! It is like a medicinal tree: if someone takes its roots, stem, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, stamens, or fruits, the tree never thinks:
‘Take the roots, but do not take the stem; take the stem, but do not take the roots.’”
"In this way, it extends even to its branches, leaves, and fruits.
Yet this medicinal tree is entirely devoid of conceptual thought, yet it is able to pacify and eliminate all the ailments—whether superior, middling, or inferior—of all sentient beings."

In this way, son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva conceives the thought of his body composed of the four great elements as a medicinal tree; according to the needs of sentient beings, he gives his hand to those who need a hand, his foot to those who need a foot, his eye to those who need an eye, his flesh to those who need flesh, his blood to those who need blood, his bone to those who need bone, his marrow to those who need marrow, his head to those who need a head, and his limbs and joints to those who need limbs and joints.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva adorns their practice of giving with such a mind, they will proceed toward inexhaustibility.

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving, they do so to cause stingy sentient beings to fulfill their generosity; to cause sentient beings with little merit to possess complete merit; to cause impoverished sentient beings to possess great fiefs; and if they give away their limbs and joints, it is to cause sentient beings to possess complete limbs and joints.”
Such giving does not direct itself toward three places.
What are these three?
It does not seek sovereign power over a kingdom; it does not seek great wealth for one's own enjoyment; and it does not direct itself toward the enlightenment of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
“Thus, this giving is for the fulfillment of the four purities.
What are the four purities? They are:
the purity of the Buddha-field, the purity of the bodhisattva-saṃgha, the purity of maturing sentient beings, and the purity of dedicating [merit] toward omniscience.”
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should thus dedicate [their merit] toward the four purities.
Furthermore, the giving of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in inexhaustibility.
What is called the "abiding in the giving" of a bodhisattva?
"Good son!
There are four kinds of giving by which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas exhaust their merit.
What are these four?
That is to say: not dedicating [the merit], lacking skillful means, having inferior intentions, and associating with evil friends.
Son of good family!
These are called the four dharmas of a bodhisattva’s giving; such giving is exhaustible.
“Good son! There are four dharmas of giving by which a bodhisattva’s generosity abides inexhaustibly.
What are these four?
That is to say: dedicating [merit] toward enlightenment, possessing skillful means, seeking to become a Dharma King, and drawing near to spiritual friends.
Son of good family!
These are called the four inexhaustible abidings in the gift of Dharma of a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, good son, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should practice giving while recollecting three things: namely, recollecting not to be separated from the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), having compassion for all sentient beings, and not contradicting the words of the Buddha while not expecting a karmic reward."
"Good son! This is called a bodhisattva practicing giving while recollecting three dharmas.
Furthermore, good son!"
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva establishes sentient beings within three dharmas while practicing giving.
What are these three? Namely:

he practices giving to establish sentient beings upon the path to bodhi; he practices giving to establish sentient beings in the well-praised Dharma; and he practices giving to establish sentient beings in the gate of the unsurpassed.
"Good son!
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva bestowing gifts while establishing sentient beings within the three dharmas.
Furthermore, good son!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice giving while aspiring for two things.
What are these two?
They are the aspiration to possess great fiefs and the ability to cultivate a mind of relinquishment.
“Good son! This is called a bodhisattva practicing giving while aspiring for two dharmas.
Furthermore, good son!”
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving in order to fulfill two dharmas, namely: knowledge (*jñāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Son of good family!
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing giving in order to fulfill these two dharmas.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva practices giving by advancing toward two dharmas.
What are these two?
That is to say, the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
Son of good family,
this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s practice of giving while advancing toward these two dharmas.
"Furthermore, good son,
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice four kinds of giving.
What are these four?
That is to say: giving with an impartial mind, giving without expectation of reward, giving directed toward bodhi, and giving that fulfills self-discipline and tranquility.
Son of good family!
These are called the four kinds of giving practiced by a bodhisattva.
"Therefore, noble son,
a bodhisattva who wishes to attain inexhaustible merit should practice such generosity as this.
At that time, the Malla Vimala addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary,
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has said that giving encompasses all the true Dharma of the Buddhas.”
“World-Honored One!
If there is a bodhisattva who accomplishes this giving, no one could measure the merit of that bodhisattva.
The Buddha said:
"So it is! So it is! Good son!"

If there is a bodhisattva who accomplishes and fulfills such generosity, know that this bodhisattva has accomplished and fulfilled an inexhaustible ocean of merit; they are not poor in the noble Dharma and have attained a great fiefdom; they abide in the stream of Dharma and have acquired great wealth; they are endowed with the seven riches and have achieved great merit; they bear the marks of a hundred blessings and serve as a great field of merit, nurturing all sentient beings.
The Scripture on the Samādhi that Collects All Merit and Virtue, Volume One;
The Scripture on the Samādhi that Collects All Merit and Virtue, Volume Two.
Translated by Kumārajīva, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Malla Śuddhatejas: "Good son, what is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s adornment of pure ethical discipline?

It means that their precepts are pure and without flaw, that they do not abandon the training in the precepts, that they have compassion for those who violate the prohibitions, and that they hold those who maintain the precepts in the highest esteem."

Purifying the three karmas of the body, purifying the four faults of speech, and purifying the three karmas of the mind; spontaneously accomplishing the ten wholesome actions and teaching others the ten wholesome actions;
not praising oneself, not giving rise to pride regarding the precepts, and diligently advancing in the cultivation of the precepts;
with a mind unmoved by the virtues of *dhūta* practices, abiding in the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) to protect one’s own mind. Not...
Seeing the faults of others, one does not commit various evils; one does not desire existence (*bhava*), nor does one take pleasure in it.
One encourages others to cultivate goodness and diligently assists them. Without longing for personal happiness, one exhorts people to practice giving (*dāna*).
One does not abandon forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka-sthāna*) and serves those who are ill. Having performed these deeds, one rejoices, acting exactly as one speaks.
He does not grieve over loss nor exult in gain; his mind remains unshaken by defamation or praise, by censure or commendation, and by suffering or pleasure.
Having severed both craving and aversion, he harbors no resentment or malice. He practices loving-kindness, viewing enemies as kin;
he does not exalt himself through precepts, nor does he turn toward other vehicles or prostrate to other deities.
Abandoning all views, coverings, obscurations, latent tendencies, and entanglements; severing and extinguishing remorse; relinquishing wealth without regret so that a heart of joy arises;
not giving rise to various thoughts and having no longing for them; enduring weariness and suffering; skillfully protecting the mind of diligence;
remaining far removed from attachment; being without alarm or fear; and [attaining] the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
“Good son! For the sake of gathering this precept, a bodhisattva mahāsattva will never violate it even at the cost of his life;
he does not maintain the prohibitive precepts for the sake of royal status, nor for the sake of being born in heaven, nor for the sake of becoming Śakra.”
The Brahma King upholds the precepts not for the sake of fiefdoms, nor for sovereignty, nor for exquisite forms;
he upholds the precepts not for the sake of physical beauty, nor for fame, nor for praise,
nor for gain, nor for honor, nor for livelihood, nor for food and drink.
One maintains the precepts not for the sake of bedding and furniture, nor for the sake of medicine for illness;

one maintains the precepts not for the sake of forms seen by the eye, sounds heard by the ear, fragrances smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, or mental phenomena cognized by the mind;
one maintains the precepts without relying upon form, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One upholds the precepts not out of reliance on the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm;
one upholds the precepts not out of fear of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals; one upholds the precepts not for the sake of seeking protection or rescue;
one upholds the precepts not out of fear of poverty and suffering in the human realm; and one upholds the precepts not out of fear of poverty and suffering in the heavenly realms.

Regarding the precepts: one upholds the prohibitions because one does not fear the poverty, suffering, and afflictions among devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, garuḍas, and mahoragas.
"One upholds the precepts for the sake of the Buddha-lineage; one upholds the precepts for the sake of abiding in and hearing the Dharma, practicing according to what has been heard;

one upholds the precepts for the sake of the Sangha-lineage; one upholds the precepts because of the desire to transcend birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; one upholds the precepts because of the desire for liberation from all..."
They uphold the precepts for the sake of sentient beings; they uphold the precepts for the sake of the peace, happiness, and benefit of all sentient beings;
they uphold the precepts because they wish to abide in the Buddha-dharma; they uphold the precepts because they wish to turn the wheel of Dharma;
they uphold the precepts in order to gather the noble lineages; and they uphold the precepts so that the lineages of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha shall not be severed.

One upholds the precepts for the sake of wondrous supernormal powers; one upholds the precepts for the sake of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
and one upholds the precepts for the sake of manifesting transformations through the bases of psychic power in boundless ways.

Thus maintaining the precepts—unbroken, unimpaired, unpierced, solid, effortless, fully accomplished, exquisite and untainted, pure and fragrant, praised by the wise, extolled by all Buddhas—one practices in accordance with the Dharma, firm and true.
"If a bodhisattva accomplishes such upholding of the precepts, they do not lose ten things.
What are these ten things? They are:
not losing the status of a wheel-turning monarch; while in that position, not giving rise to negligence; aspiring to attain unsurpassed enlightenment; and wishing to behold the Buddhas."
Not losing the status of Śakra, once having attained this state, they do not give rise to negligence; they aspire to attain unsurpassed bodhi and vow to behold the Buddha.
Not losing the status of a Brahmā King, once being in this state, they do not give rise to negligence; they aspire to attain unsurpassed bodhi and vow to behold the Buddha.
With pure faith in what is correct and true, they do not lose the opportunity to hear the Dharma.
They are well able to discern the Dharma as it has been heard;
they do not lose the grasping of bodhisattva wisdom;
and they do not lose their uninterrupted and unimpeded eloquence.
They do not lose the accumulation of all roots of goodness;
they do not lose that which is praised by all Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas;
and they do not lose the swift ability to penetrate the wisdom of all Buddhas.
If a bodhisattva accomplishes such upholding of the precepts, they shall not lose these ten dharmas.

When a bodhisattva accomplishes such a collection of morality, the devas constantly pay them homage; the nāgas revere and respect them; the yakṣas constantly make offerings to them; and the gandharvas also constantly make offerings. The asuras serve them with respect, while kings, brahmins, elders, and householders all honor them.
The wise always approach them; the Buddhas always keep them in mind; and the devas and people of the world always serve them as their teachers, constantly taking pity on sentient beings.
“If a bodhisattva thus maintains the aggregate of pure ethical discipline, they will not be reborn in four places—except for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
What are these four?

They will not be reborn in border regions; they will not be reborn in lands where no Buddha resides; they will not be reborn into families with wrong views; and they will not be reborn in the evil destinies.”
In this way, the Bodhisattva who purely maintains the aggregate of ethical discipline does not take birth in the four states of existence.
Furthermore, son of good family,
the Bodhisattva who purely maintains the aggregate of ethical discipline does not lose four dharmas.
What are these four? They are:

not losing the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), not losing the mindfulness of the Buddha, not losing the hearing of the Dharma, and having heard the Dharma, not forgetting it for as long as immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas. These are the four dharmas that constitute the Bodhisattva’s pure accumulation of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha) without loss.

“Good son! If a bodhisattva thus purely guards the aggregate of precepts, they will not encounter four situations: they will not encounter the extinction of the Dharma, nor the kalpa of weapons, nor the kalpa of famine, nor the kalpa of conflagration.”
When a bodhisattva thus purely maintains the aggregate of ethical discipline, they do not encounter these four [adversities].
Furthermore, son of good family,
when a bodhisattva thus purely maintains the aggregate of ethical discipline, they attain four supreme dharmas.
That is to say: not deceiving the Buddhas, not deceiving the devas, not deceiving sentient beings, and not deceiving one's own mind.
When a bodhisattva thus purely maintains the aggregate of ethical discipline, they attain these four supreme dharmas.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva who accomplishes the protection and maintenance of the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha) is free from ten kinds of fear.
What are these ten?

They are free from the fear of hell; free from the fear of the animal realm; free from the fear of hungry ghosts; free from the fear of poverty; free from the fear of ill repute; free from the fear of the various fetters (*paryavasthāna*); free from the fear of the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; free from the fear of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas, and so forth; free from the fear of executioners, swords, staves, fire, poison, and the like; and free from the fear of lions, tigers, leopards, bears, brown bears, *tarakṣus*, foxes, wolves, pythons, cats, mice, centipedes, venomous snakes, gadflies, mosquitoes, kings, and thieves.
In this way, the bodhisattva abiding in the aggregate of pure ethical discipline is free from the ten kinds of fear. "Good son!
When a bodhisattva maintains the precepts, they are able to give rise to all Buddha-dharmas, even up to the arising of unsurpassed bodhi."

Why is this? Because if one upholds the precepts, there is samādhi; if one upholds the precepts, there is wisdom; if one upholds the precepts, there is liberation; and if one upholds the precepts, there is the knowledge and vision of liberation.
“Good son! What is called ‘precept’?
A precept is that which pacifies and subdues the fetters and afflictions.”
For what reason are they called fetters and latent tendencies?
They are called fetters and latent tendencies because they defile all sentient beings within the three realms of existence.
What is meant by "quiescence"?

To be without false conceptualization, without discrimination, and without attachment, never thinking of any phenomena—this is called the complete pacification and subduing of all fetters and afflictions.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cannot thus know the pacification and subduing of the fetters and latent tendencies, this is not called the purity of the aggregate of ethical discipline.”

Why is this? If one cannot know how to pacify and subdue the fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), then even if one is born in the Brahma world, one remains defiled by those fetters; this continues even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), where one still remains subject to those fetters.
“Good son! For this reason, you should know that the quiescence of the fetters of the three realms is called the aggregate of pure precepts.
At that time, the Malla Śuddhatejas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If being free from the defilements of the fetters within the triple world is called the aggregate of pure precepts, why did the World-Honored One, while still a bodhisattva, leave behind the fetters of the triple world yet still take birth therein?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Malla Vīrabala: "Good son!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not take birth within the triple world through his own fetters; rather, by means of skillful means, he dwells within the triple world while remaining free from the fetters of the triple world, for the sake of transforming sentient beings."
"Good son!
Suppose that humans or devas were able to paint all manner of forms and images within empty space;
what do you think? Would this not be rare?"
"So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata!
What this person has done is truly most rare."
The Buddha said,
“Good son! That a bodhisattva abandons all fetters and afflictions, yet dwells within the triple world and manifests the transformations of the three vehicles— this is truly rare.”
The Mārapramardaka Vīra said:
“World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva has accomplished the dwelling in the gates of liberation, yet out of compassion for sentient beings, he returns to dwell within the triple world.”
“World-Honored One!
It is as if there were a person who, having escaped with his life and body intact from the hands of an executioner, returned to that place and said to him:
‘You have now killed me; do not kill anyone else.’”
"World-Honored One!

These three realms are like the house of an executioner; all sentient beings are like those destined for death; the various conditioned phenomena of birth and death are like the executioner; and those who have escaped from them are like Bodhisattvas who, having already transcended the three realms, return to dwell within them in order to transform sentient beings and liberate them."
World-Honored One!
This great compassion of the bodhisattva is beyond the reach of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?
“Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas lack this great compassion, lack skillful means, and lack the adornment of pure precepts.
The World-Honored One further addressed the Malla Netrī: “Good son!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully cultivate and accumulate the adornment of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), and how does he seek and study that extensive learning?
Son of good family!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva, toward his preceptors (*upādhyāya*) and instructors (*ācārya*), shows reverence, makes offerings, respects, and praises them; he acts according to their instructions, abandons pride, and quickly receives their teachings. He conceives of the true Dharma as medicine, conceives of his preceptors and instructors as Buddhas, conceives of himself as a patient, and conceives of the teacher of the Dharma as a skilled physician. For the sake of gathering the Buddha-dharmas, he does not cherish his own body or life, and regarding all surplus wealth, robes, and alms bowls, he conceives of them as causes for affliction and bondage.

Although they possess hereditary fiefs and emoluments, they do not give rise to attachment; for the sake of honoring the Dharma, they relinquish everything; to protect the True Dharma, they should renounce all worldly treasures; to attain the Dharma, they should renounce all fame and praise; and to become a Dharma King, they renounce all royal thrones.
In order to abandon all fetters and latent tendencies, one should diligently cultivate the application of the Dharma;
in order to rescue all sentient beings, one should diligently cultivate the application of the Dharma.
When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas cultivate and gather all dharmas, they naturally attain all roots of goodness.
Therefore, sons of good family,
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to realize bodhi and wish to erect the pillar of wisdom should cultivate extensive learning.
“Good son! Just as the Hall of Śakra remains stable by means of its pillars, and the Thirty-three Gods rejoice within it,
so too, good son!”
By means of the pillar of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom, all devas and people of the world receive and enjoy happiness. "Good son!

If there is a bodhisattva who has resolved upon bodhicitta and, being embraced by bodhi, declares his intent to become a Buddha, yet does not diligently cultivate extensive learning, he is the most ignorant among all sentient beings."
Therefore, son of good family,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should diligently apply themselves with vigor to cultivate and accumulate extensive learning, becoming a pillar of learning among all sentient beings.
At that time, all the devas were filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
This virtuous man, having cultivated wisdom through steadfast and firm diligence, will surely attain the ten powers of a Buddha;
this virtuous man shall, by the power of wisdom, sever the net of all fetters.
This virtuous man shall expound the Dharma to sever all the fetters and afflictions of sentient beings;
this virtuous man shall proceed to the foot of that Bodhi tree where the Buddhas sit;
this virtuous man shall, by his own power, subdue all Māras.
This virtuous man shall turn the Dharma wheel of twelve aspects. "Good son!

When a bodhisattva cultivates extensive learning, all the palaces of Māra are completely shrouded in darkness, and the Māras of the trichiliocosm all become distressed and troubled, saying these words:"
"This person now surpasses us," said the other celestial Māras, each speaking these words:
"This person has subdued our lord; we all belong entirely to this person."

"Why is this? Good son! Because by means of this bodhisattva’s accumulation of wisdom from extensive learning, he is able to pacify the fetters; since there are no fetters, Māra finds no opportunity."
Having already attained much learning, one is able to discern; being able to discern, one is able to practice; having already been able to practice, Māra finds no opportunity.

One who cultivates much learning remains far removed from wrong views and attains right view; having already attained right abiding, Māra finds no opportunity, and thus one is able to practice rightly.
Having already been able to practice rightly, one is able to discern the meaning and abandon all that is non-meaningful, thereby being able to correctly transcend both meaning and non-meaning.
“Good son! For these reasons, you should understand it thus. Good son!”
When a bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates this great learning, they eliminate the four kinds of māras:
namely, the māra of the aggregates (skandhamāra), the māra of afflictions (kleśamāra), the māra of death (mṛtyumāra), and the māra of the devas (devaputramāra). "Good son!
As it was when the Bodhisattva originally gathered extensive learning—desiring the Dharma, benefiting from the Dharma, and dwelling well within the Dharma—I shall now speak briefly.
"Good son!..."
In the past, incalculable, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago,
there was a great seer named Jyeṣṭha who dwelt in the mountain forests, possessed the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and constantly practiced a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
He formed this thought:

"My current cultivation of a mind of loving-kindness in the mountains yields no benefit; for it is not merely a mind of loving-kindness that can extinguish the afflictions accumulated by sentient beings over immeasurable eons—it is not this loving-kindness that can give rise to right view."
Again, he thought:
"By means of what thing can right view be aroused?
Having formed this thought, he said:
"There are two causes and conditions that can give rise to right view:
namely, hearing from others and, having heard, reflecting correctly.
By means of these two factors, one can produce right view."
At that time, he gave rise to the aspiration for extensive learning, thinking:
"From where shall I hear well-spoken teachings, so that through the causal conditions of the Dharma, I may gather the factors corresponding to the Dharma?"

"At that time, the rishi traveled to various villages, fiefdoms, districts, counties, and royal cities, searching everywhere for one of great learning; yet he was utterly unable to find a teacher who could preach the Dharma."
At that time, a son of Māra came to his place and spoke these words:
"I now have a single verse spoken by the Buddha.
Upon hearing the name of the Buddha's verse, this most excellent sage immediately said to him:
"Please expound it for me.
Then the deva replied,
"If you can now flay your skin to serve as paper, use your blood as ink, and break your bones to serve as pens to transcribe this verse, I shall then grant you the verse spoken by the Buddha."
“Good son! At that time, the Most Victorious Sage (Varasvāmin) thought to himself:

‘Throughout immeasurable births and deaths, in every place where I was born, I have for hundreds of thousands of kalpas constantly fallen into the hands of robbers, soldiers, and executioners even when there was no cause. With sharp blades they cut me and dismembered my limbs; whether for the sake of desire or for the sake of wealth and profit, they killed, bound, beat, imprisoned, and reviled me. I underwent immeasurable suffering without any benefit, receiving these cuts and severings in vain.’”
"I shall now exchange this non-substantial body for the attainment of the sublime Dharma.
Rejoicing and leaping for joy, thinking "I have gained a great benefit," upon hearing these words of the Dharma, he conceived toward that deity the notion of a teacher and a spiritual guide.

He then took a sharp knife and flayed his own skin, drying it to serve as paper; he pierced himself to draw blood for ink; and he broke his bones and shaved them down to fashion pens. Joining his palms toward the heavens, he spoke these words:
"O Heaven, speak to me the verses attained by the Buddha."
“As previously commanded, I have already completed all tasks: flaying my skin for paper, drawing blood for ink, and breaking my bones for pens.
“Good son! [The Buddha said:]
At that time, the Māra-devaputra, seeing the Most Victorious Seer (Jinvarṣi) reverently honoring the Dharma, became distressed upon seeing this and immediately vanished.
"O son of good family!
When the Most Victorious Seer saw the deva disappear, he thought to himself:"

"I now give rise to a mind of reverence for the Dharma; I shall flay my skin to make paper and break my bones to make pens. As I thus seek the Dharma with such reverence, these roots of goodness shall never perish."

If these words of mine are truthful and not false, and if I have given rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings, sparing neither body nor life, then let my skin be peeled off to serve as paper, my blood shed to serve as ink, and my bones broken to serve as pens.
"If my heart is sincere, truthful, and not false, may those who possess great kindness and great compassion and are able to preach the Dharma in other world-realms appear before me. "Good son!"

When the Great Seer Uttara had spoken these words, in a single moment of thought, thirty-two Buddha-fields to the east of this buddha-field, there was a land named Samantavimalā. Therein dwelt a Buddha named Vimalakīrtirāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is currently present. Knowing the thoughts and intentions of the Great Seer Uttara, and desiring likewise to transform the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa, he traveled through the air and arrived before the Great Seer Uttara in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, accompanied by five hundred bodhisattvas.

The Tathāgata King of Pure Fame emitted a great radiance that shone everywhere throughout that grove; the heavens rained down various flowers, and at that time, the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of those trees all produced the sounds of the Dharma.
At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of devas gathered together.
Then, once that rishi had been touched by the light of the Buddha Pure Name King, all his suffering was entirely eliminated; he returned to his former state, without any trace of scars.
