At that time, the seer bowed his head in respectful salutation at the feet of the Buddha, the World-Honored One; he circumambulated him three times to the right, joined his palms above his head, and addressed the Buddha, King of Pure Name, saying:
"World-Honored One, you are my teacher!"
"The Sugata is my teacher!
World-Honored One, I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha. I only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma for me."

Having heard the Dharma, I preach it for the sake of guiding those sentient beings who lack faith, who practice wrong views, who destroy right view, and who walk in darkness, so that they may be shown the correct path.

“Good son! At that time, King Vimalaprabhā Buddha, for the sake of the supreme seer, the various devaputras, the bodhisattvas, and others, expounded for them this dharma of the Samādhi of Gathering All Merit.”
Among that assembly of devas, eight thousand sons of gods who had originally planted roots of goodness all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path;
the Most Victorious Great Seer attained great joy, gave birth to great faith, and obtained unimpeded eloquence.
"That Buddha-Tathāgata further expounded for them the eight adamantine phrases (*vajrapada*).
What are the eight?
The phrase that the nature of all dharmas is fundamentally pure, because all dharmas are free from fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana-kleśa*);..."
All phenomena are phrases of outflowlessness, for they exhaust all outflows;
all phenomena are phrases of being free from nests and dens, for they have transcended nests and dens;
all phenomena are phrases of having no gate, for there is no duality.
All phenomena are phrases of universality, because they reveal the gates of liberation;
all phenomena are phrases of no-going, because there is no place to go;
all phenomena are phrases of no-coming, because all comings have been severed.
The phrase "all phenomena are equal throughout the three periods of time" is because the past, future, and present lack dualistic characteristics.
That King Vimalakīrti Buddha expounded these eight adamantine phrases, through which the meaning of all phenomena is elucidated and understood.
Furthermore, he expounded eight other Dharma-gates to enable Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to swiftly achieve wisdom.
What are these eight?
They are: the gate of names for all dharmas, because all dharmas are distinguished by means of names;
The gateway of the sounds and voices of all phenomena, because they bring joy through verbal differentiation;
the gateway of the common conventions of all phenomena, because all phenomena possess a determinate nature;
the gateway of the speech of all phenomena, because they are sovereign over falsehood.
All phenomena are the gate of self-characteristics, because they are free from other characteristics;
all phenomena are the gate of ultimate exhaustion, because they are non-existent;
all phenomena are the gate of discrimination, because they arise from discrimination.
The gate of the equality of all phenomena, because they are of one and the same flavor.
Most Excellent One!
This is called the eightfold gate of swiftly accomplishing wisdom.
“Most Excellent One!
Furthermore, there is an eight-syllable seed-gateway that can accomplish inexhaustible eloquence.
What are these eight?
The seed-syllable gate of the letter A for all phenomena demonstrates that phenomena are unarisen;
the seed-syllable gate of the letter Śa for all phenomena demonstrates the ultimate truth (paramārtha-dharma);
the seed-syllable gate of the letter Na for all phenomena demonstrates the designation of names and forms (nāmarūpa).
The seed-syllable gate of the letter *cha* for all phenomena demonstrates the subduing of all phenomena;
the seed-syllable gate of the letter *va* for all phenomena demonstrates the entry of all phenomena into equality;
the seed-syllable gate of the letter *ta* for all phenomena demonstrates the indestructibility of suchness.
All phenomena are the seed-gateway of the syllable KA, because it extinguishes the karma of suffering;
all phenomena are the seed-gateway of the syllable MA, because it ultimately accomplishes the severance of all phenomena.
This is called the gateway of the eight-syllable seed-mantra, which can accomplish inexhaustible eloquence; therefore, it is most supreme.

One should practice with right mindfulness this gateway of the eight-syllable seed-mantra, the gateway of the eight dharmas, and the gateway of the eight vajra-phrases; always remaining free from clamor and bustle, constantly reflecting well, and observing, cultivating, and accumulating the benefits of merit.

“Good son! After the Tathāgata King of Pure Fame had spoken this Dharma, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated the entire world and caused the great earth to tremble; he then vanished from sight and returned to his own land together with the bodhisattvas, yet none of those sentient beings were aware of the Buddha’s coming or going.”

“Good son! At that time, the Great Seer Most Victorious (Vijayin) attained noble eloquence. With the gods attending upon him and the gods guarding him for the sake of subduing Māra, he traveled to various villages, cities, kingdoms, and towns, extensively expounding and proclaiming this Samādhi of the Accumulation of All Merit for the sake of all sentient beings.”

For a full thousand years he constantly expounded the Dharma, causing eighty-four thousand sentient beings to abide in the Śrāvaka vehicle, eighty-four thousand sentient beings to abide in the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, eighty-four thousand sentient beings to abide in the Mahāyāna; eighty-four thousand sentient beings became Cakravartin kings, eighty-four thousand sentient beings became Śakra-devānām-indra, eighty-four thousand sentient beings attained the status of Brahmā kings; eighty-four thousand sentient beings practiced loving-kindness (*maitrī*), eighty-four thousand sentient beings practiced compassion (*karuṇā*), eighty-four thousand sentient beings practiced sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and eighty-four thousand sentient beings practiced equanimity (*upekṣā*); and immeasurable sentient beings were reborn in the heavens.
"This Most Supreme Great Sage passed away and was immediately reborn in that Land of Universal Purity of King of Pure Names Buddha, and eighty-four thousand devaputras were also reborn in that land."
“Good son! What do you think?
Was the supreme seer at that time anyone other than this person?”
Do not harbor any doubt; it was I myself who was then.
Because I originally cherished the Dharma and revered the Dharma, and because I spoke words of truth, I was able to reverently move that Buddha King Pure Name to come to my presence.
Therefore, you should know that if there is a bodhisattva who reverently seeks the Dharma, for that person the Buddha does not enter parinirvāṇa, nor does the Dharma perish. Why is this?
"Viśuddhatejas!

If there are bodhisattvas who are single-mindedly devoted to accomplishing the quest for the True Dharma, even though they reside in a different land, they will always behold the Buddha face-to-face and hear the True Dharma."
Vimalatejas!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva desires the Dharma and reveres the Dharma, they shall cause all mountain crags, trees, forests, and thickets to produce the dharma-treasury dhāraṇī-gates, and various sūtra scrolls will come of their own accord into their hands.
"Viśuddhatejas!

Whenever there are bodhisattvas who revere the Dharma and desire the Dharma, if any devas who have previously seen a Buddha come to their presence, they shall fully expound for them all the various dharmas that they heard from the Buddha."
"Pure Splendor!

If the lifespan of a Bodhisattva who benefits the Dharma comes to an end, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, shall extend his life. Sustained by the power of the Buddhas, if he wishes to remain for a thousand years, he can indeed remain; likewise for two thousand, three thousand, four thousand, or five thousand years, even up to one kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa—he can abide as he desires."
“Viśuddhatejas!
If there is a bodhisattva who reveres the Dharma and desires the Dharma, they will not grow old nor fall ill; they will attain the power of mindfulness, advance toward wisdom, and acquire eloquence.”
If there is a bodhisattva who reveres the Dharma and desires the Dharma, and having seen the Buddha, abandons all views and enters into right view—
Pure Splendor!
If there is a bodhisattva who reveres the Dharma and desires the Dharma, no sentient beings whatsoever will be able to harm them.
"Therefore, Viśuddhatejas!
This great being should diligently cultivate the adornment of extensive learning; the merit he shall obtain will surpass even this.
Viśuddhatejas!"

If there are bodhisattvas who abide in these three adornments of merit—whose pillars of merit are vast, whose merit increases, whose merit is inexhaustible, and whose merit is inconceivable—no one will be able to reach the limit of such merit.
"Viśuddhatejas!

One might be able to count the drops of the great ocean with a single hair, but no one can exhaustively reach the limit of this bodhisattva’s accumulation of merit from adornment, nor his accumulation of pure precepts, extensive learning, and wisdom."
“Śuddhatejas!

One may be able to weigh the grasses, trees, mountains, forests, and all sentient beings within a trichiliocosm and thus determine their weight, but one cannot measure the mass of merit, precepts, learning, and wisdom of such a bodhisattva’s adornment and reach its limit; this is called the explanation of the adornment of knowledge.”
At that time, the Malla Śuddhatejas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Among these three adornments—the adornment of generosity, the adornment of pure precepts, and the adornment of extensive learning—which is the most supreme?”
"Which is superior?
The Buddha said,
"Viśuddhatejas!"
Among the three adornments, the adornment of extensive learning is most worthy of praise, most supreme and exalted, unsurpassed, and the highest of the high.
"O Son of Good Family!
Just as a single mustard seed might be placed upon the side of Mount Sumeru, so too are the merit of this giving and the aggregate of pure precepts like that mustard seed;
whereas the adornment of extensive learning is like Mount Sumeru itself.
"Noble son!
Just as there is the space occupied by a single small bird, so too is the adornment of generosity and ethical discipline;
the adornment of extensive learning is like the remaining space."
“Good son! The adornment of giving can accomplish two things.
What are these two?
It can eliminate poverty and bring about great wealth and status.
Adornment through pure precepts also performs two functions.
What are these two?
First, one leaves the evil realms; second, one reaches the place of goodness.
Son of good family!
Adornment through extensive learning also performs two functions.
What are these two?
They are: being able to eliminate all views, and being able to accumulate the adornments of all wisdom. Good son!
The adornment of generosity is a tainted retribution; the adornment of pure ethical discipline is also a tainted retribution.
Noble son! The adornment of extensive learning is untainted and without retribution.
"Therefore, noble son,
a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should diligently apply themselves with vigor to cultivate the wisdom of extensive learning.

When this Dharma of the adornments of the merit of giving, pure precepts, and extensive learning was spoken, three thousand sentient beings who had originally planted roots of goodness immediately gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment.
Five thousand devaputras became free from dust and defilement regarding all dharmas and attained the pure Dharma-eye;
the Māraputra Viśuddhatejas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, the Māraputra Viśuddhatejas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By accomplishing how many dharmas can a bodhisattva-mahāsattva swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
What are these four?

That is to say, Pure Splendor! one understands that the body is like a reflection in a mirror, understands that speech is like an echo, understands that the mind is like an illusion, and understands that all phenomena are non-dual.
It should be known that if a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they will swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena.
What are the four? They are:

first, compassion that universally covers all sentient beings while maintaining no notion of "sentient beings"; second, understanding the emptiness of all phenomena while not perceiving anything to be understood; third, beholding the purity of the Buddha through the wisdom-eye rather than the flesh-eye; and fourth, skillfully discerning the mind while neither seeing the mind nor relying upon it.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they will swiftly attain the endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Furthermore, good son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
What are these four?
They are: not abandoning any sentient being, relinquishing all views, upholding pure precepts, and pacifying all fetters.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they will swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, good son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they can swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
What are these four? They are:
possessing the power of patience, the progressive increase of the Dharma, diligent application of vigor, and understanding the tranquility of phenomena.
"Noble son!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they can swiftly attain the patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they can swiftly attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
What are these four? They are:

attaining dhyāna without relying on dhyāna; discerning with wisdom that there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); accomplishing skillful means to gather in sentient beings; and increasing all practices while possessing thorough knowledge of those practices.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they will swiftly attain the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, good son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
What are these four? They are:

saving all sentient beings through great loving-kindness; not wearying of birth and death through great compassion; rejoicing in the Dharma through great sympathetic joy; and severing all craving through great equanimity.
"Noble son!
A bodhisattva who accomplishes these four dharmas can swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will swiftly attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
What are these four? They are:
attaining the three gates of liberation; understanding and knowing the three periods of time; transcending the three realms; and having faith that the nature of phenomena is non-arising.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they will swiftly attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

While he was thus expounding these four dharmas, the Malla Vimala attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; filled with joy and exultation, he rose into the air to the height of seven *tāla* trees.
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; the music of humans and devas played simultaneously, celestial flowers fell like clouds, and a great light shone universally throughout this world.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they smile, hundreds of thousands of rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and purple—issue from their mouth and illuminate immeasurable and boundless worlds. They pass upward beyond the Brahma world, then return, circling the body three times before re-entering through the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head.
Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; for what reason, World-Honored One, do you smile now?
He asked in verse, saying:
"Having attained supreme wisdom and the stainless eye, With all faculties stilled, you have reached the further shore."
With a great radiance like the color of Mount Sumeru, for what cause and condition does the Guide smile?
You who well know the faculties and conducts of sentient beings, whose pure wisdom corresponds with the knowledge of the three periods of time,
and who have attained the supreme wisdom of non-conceptualization— O you whose face is like the full moon, please explain the reason for your smile.
Just as the Buddhas of the past and those of the future, so too are the Honored Buddhas of the present;
through their various true and pure practices, they thoroughly know the reality of all things as they truly are.
His body pervades all Buddha-fields, and his voice likewise fills all Buddha-fields;
his heart of loving-kindness pervades all sentient beings—pray tell, who is endowed with such wisdom?
The Sovereign One knows all phenomena to be like the moon in water, Like illusory transformations and likewise like a dream;
Like space, like lightning—these pure phenomena. For what reason does the Lion among Men smile now?

Having realized the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and skillfully knowing true nature while always taming the mind, you move like the wind through the void; I pray that you explain for what reason you smile.
Now, with his Buddha-wisdom, who does the Buddha know in his heart?
Who shall descend at the Tree of Enlightenment to subdue Māra?
And who shall sit upon the Vajrāsana?
O Immortal among Men, for what reason do you smile now?
This is not within the realm of the śrāvakas, nor is it accessible to the pratyekabuddhas;
it is the ocean-like realm of the Buddha’s wisdom. We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for this.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
“Ānanda, do you now see this Māhāsthāmaprāpta, the Māhavīrya, abiding in the void? “Ānanda! [the Buddha continued.]

After three hundred billion *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, this Māhāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva shall attain Buddhahood, appearing in the world as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Bahuvyūharāja. This shall occur in the eastern direction in a land called Vyūhaśuddhā and in an eon called Brahmastava.

Ānanda, you should know that this King Mahāvyūha shall attain Buddhahood in a land of pure adornment; that realm will be abundant, joyful, peaceful, and flourishing, and the objects of enjoyment for its inhabitants will be like those of the Tuṣita Heaven.
This Buddha, King Adorned, does not preach any other Dharma but solely the Bodhisattva Vehicle;
there is not even the name of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha Vehicles. The assembly consists purely of Bodhisattvas who have all attained the patient acceptance of dharmas (dharmakṣānti).
There are none of the eight difficulties, nor are there any Māras, enemies, or followers of external paths.
"The lifespan of that Buddha is immeasurable; his land is made of lapis lazuli, interspersed with flowers of Jambu-river gold.

At that time, the Malla Vīrabala descended from the air, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, requested to leave the household life. The Buddha immediately granted his permission.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, this is unprecedented!
Sugata, this is unprecedented!”

Thus, by means of these supreme and wondrous wholesome dharmas, he skillfully disciplines sentient beings, even those who are so arrogant and competitive that when they encounter the Buddha-Tathāgata, they immediately attain joy, abandon their arrogance, and prostrate at the Tathāgata’s feet.

When this Great Arrogant Malla, Pure Majesty, has abandoned his arrogance and attained the supreme Dharma, he shall further subdue immeasurable sentient beings and cause them to abandon their pride and arrogance.
"Bhagavān! How many Buddhas has this Mārapramardaka Māra-powerful One previously made offerings to? Bhagavān!
Having planted what roots of goodness is he able to attain such swift understanding?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa: “Nārāyaṇa!
This Māhārāja Śuddhabala once, in past ages, made offerings to sixty-two billion buddhas and planted various roots of goodness.”

From this day forward, you shall again encounter immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable buddhas, whom you shall revere, make offerings to, honor, and praise, while purely cultivating the holy life.
Nārāyaṇa said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does this Māhātmya-mahāsthāma-malla harbor such great arrogance as to seek to compete with the Buddha for superiority?”
The Buddha told Nārāyaṇa:
“There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva forgets the bodhicitta.
What are these four?
Namely: overweening pride, lack of reverence for the Dharma, disparaging spiritual friends, and speaking untruths.
Nārāyaṇa! When a bodhisattva possesses these four qualities, they forget the bodhicitta.
"Nārāyaṇa! Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva forgets the bodhicitta. They are:
praising those who incline toward the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; disparaging the Mahāyāna; reviling bodhisattvas; and being stingy with the Dharma."
"Nārāyaṇa! A bodhisattva who possesses these four qualities forgets the bodhicitta. Nārāyaṇa!"
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva forgets the bodhicitta.
What are these four?

Practicing deceptive and delusive arts toward sentient beings; feigning intimacy through fraudulence; engaging in hypocritical speech with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); and doing so for the sake of gain and sustenance.
"Nārāyaṇa! A bodhisattva who possesses these four dharmas forgets the bodhicitta. Nārāyaṇa!"
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva forgets the bodhicitta.
What are these four?
Not recognizing the deeds of Māra; not eliminating karmic obstructions; having a weak and feeble will; and lacking skillful means and wisdom.
"Nārāyaṇa! A bodhisattva who possesses these four dharmas forgets the bodhicitta. Nārāyaṇa!"
This Mārapramardana, the Māra-powerful One, originally committed evil karma and forgot his bodhicitta.
I shall now speak; listen well to me.
"In the distant past, within this Bhadrakalpa, there appeared a Buddha in the world named Kākutsunda."
Within this Buddha-dharma, there was a great brahmin named Sudhana, who gave rise to great arrogance and attained overweening pride, and thus did not go to the place where the Buddha was.
Due to excessive pride, he enters into disputes and competition with those brahmins who preach the Dharma to kings.

Because of this pride, he incurs retribution in the present life and suffers the loss of many things—namely, he does not see the Buddha, he does not hear the True Dharma, nor does he hear the Mahāyāna teachings that lead toward bodhisattvahood; furthermore, he does not hear the pure dharmas of the devas, nor does he hear of meritorious roots dedicated toward awakening.
Because these five unwholesome factors obstruct and maintain him, he becomes estranged from the bodhicitta.
"Nārāyaṇa! What do you think?
Was the Brahmin Sudhana at that time someone other than this person?"
Do not harbor any doubt; it was this very Māṇava Śuddhasthāma who was then.
Because of his arrogance, he forgot the bodhicitta;
yet, because of the original roots of goodness of that bodhicitta, he did not fall into the evil realms.
Although they have attained great power, they still possess arrogance.
Sustained by the Buddha’s power, they hear of the Buddha’s power and the power of the bodhisattvas; thus, they abandon their pride and will come to see the Buddha in the future.

"By not committing any evils and by virtue of fundamental roots of goodness that have now been activated, one swiftly attains this patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa said to the Malla Viśuddhatejas:
"In what dharma do you abide to attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena and receive this prediction (*vyākaraṇa*)?"
Viśuddhatejas replied,
“I have received the prediction of enlightenment by giving rise to the dharmas of ordinary beings. Nārāyaṇa said:
"How is it that they arise?
Viśuddhatejas replied, "They arise as if not arising; in this way they arise."
"Extinction is like non-extinction; it is thus extinguished.
It is thus born, and likewise does not abide. Nārāyaṇa said:
“Good son! If that were so, what difference would there be between the Buddha-dharma and the dharma of ordinary persons?
Viśuddatejas replied:
"It is only because of words that there is distinction; if one considers their meaning, there is no distinction.
Nārāyaṇa said: "What meaning is there in these dharmas of ordinary beings?"
Viśuddhatejas replied:
"The absence of conceptual construction and the absence of discrimination—this is the meaning of the dharmas of ordinary beings. Nārāyaṇa said:
"What is the purport of this meaning?
Viśuddhatejas replied, "As for this meaning,
it is to depart from the dharmas of ordinary beings and proceed toward the Buddha-dharmas."
Nārāyaṇa asked, "What is the meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
Viśuddhatejas replied:
"Not performing duality is the meaning of the Buddha-dharma," Nārāyaṇa said. "Good son!"
As the Buddha has taught, one should rely on the Dharma and not on the person.
Furthermore, he said that there are two causes and conditions for the arising of right view. What are these two?
"Because of external sounds and internal skillful reflection, such meanings are themselves the letters.
Viśuddhatejas replied, "Nārāyaṇa!..."
In accordance with the Dharma, a bodhisattva does not grasp at words nor does he grasp at non-words.
If one attains words, that itself constitutes the meaning; yet that which is the meaning is the non-attainment of meaning.
Therefore, one does not rely on meaning, for all dharmas are entirely devoid of meaning.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are unattainable; they are neither spatial nor separate from space, and wherever they abide, they are extinguished right there.
As the Buddha has taught, the ultimate cessation of all conceptualization is what is called "meaning.

Therefore, Nārāyaṇa, for one who relies on meaning, there is nothing that can be relied upon and nothing that cannot be relied upon; this reliance on neither-reliance-nor-non-reliance is what is called "meaning."
Nārāyaṇa said: "Good son!
Is there not the case where relying upon meaning is itself relying upon all dharmas?"
Viśuddhatejas said:
"There is, Nārāyaṇa!"
All phenomena are empty; all phenomena are quiescent.
All phenomena are empty, and their basis is likewise so;
all phenomena are quiescent, and their basis is likewise so.
"In this way, Nārāyaṇa!
If one relies on this meaning, one relies upon all dharmas.
Nārāyaṇa said:
"Viśuddhavīrya! If it is so, then all dharmas are eternally and naturally their own support.
Viśuddhavīrya replied:
"So it is, so it is! Nārāyaṇa!
All dharmas are the ultimate truth."
Those who rely on the ultimate truth (paramārtha) shall attain peace and happiness; they should therefore seek the ultimate truth.

If one can give rise to neither dharma nor non-dharma, seeking neither duality nor non-duality, this is called the noble discernment and selection. Yet, this selection is without action and without non-action.
"If there is neither doing nor non-doing, this is called 'doing'; thus, the meanings of 'that which is sought' and 'the seeker' are not mutually contradictory.
When the Mārapramardaka Vīra expounded this Dharma, five hundred bhikṣus did not grasp at any dharmas, their outflows were exhausted, and their minds attained liberation;
eight thousand devaputras were distanced from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa said to the Malla Śuddhasthāman:

“As the Buddha has taught, one should rely on the meaning and not on the letter; yet these sentient beings do not understand this meaning and practice according to two [extremes]. Thus, they neither understand the letter nor understand the meaning.”
Because of this lack of understanding, it is said that one should rely on the meaning and not on the letter.
To rely on the letter and to rely on the meaning—the meaning transcends all written words. "Good son!
As the Buddha has taught, there are two causes and conditions that can give rise to right view.

That is to say, there may be someone who has not heard the true Dharma; within the Dharma of discipline, due to some minor circumstance, they immediately feel joy and say, "I have escaped from birth and death. This is overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

"This was originally due to overweening pride; however, in order to exhort this person to practice diligently, once they have heard the Dharma, they will immediately begin to practice and proceed toward the right path."
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"Having heard, one comes to know the Dharma; having heard, one does not commit evil; having heard, one abandons what is unbeneficial; having heard, one attains Nirvana."
Nārāyaṇa asked: "How does a bhikṣu practice mindfulness associated with the Dharma?
Viśuddhatejas replied:
"There is neither association nor non-association; if one can be thus, this is association with the mindfulness of the Dharma.
Nārāyaṇa said: "That practitioner is associated with speech."
"Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa!
If there is a bhikṣu who is in accord with mindfulness of the Dharma, he will give rise to neither anger nor pride; this is called right reflection."

"If one observes the teachings regarding the past, future, and present, and understands what is taught—that they are taught for the sake of abandonment, for the sake of understanding, and for the sake of cultivation—and does not apprehend anything done in the past, does not apprehend anything to be done in the future, and does not apprehend anything being done in the present, this is right practice."
"If one correctly contemplates that the nature of all phenomena is eternally extinguished, this is called the vision attained through correct cultivation of reflection;
if one sees that the nature of all phenomena is eternally tranquil, this is called the vision attained through the cultivation of correct reflection;
if one correctly contemplates that the nature of all phenomena is eternally concentrated, this is called the vision attained through the cultivation of correct reflection."
If one correctly contemplates that all phenomena are ultimately unarisen, this is called the vision attained through the cultivation of right reflection;
if one correctly contemplates that all phenomena are truly impermanent, this is called the vision attained through the cultivation of right reflection;
if one correctly contemplates that all phenomena are impermanent and subject to cessation, this is called the vision attained through the cultivation of right reflection.
"If that which sees and that which is seen are both entirely unobservable—seeing as suchness (tathatā) and yet not seeing—this is called the teaching and demonstration of contemplation."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Māraputra Śuddhasthāmaprāpta:
"Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!"
What you have said is thus consistent with reality.
If one can act in this way, then there will be no delusion regarding all phenomena;
practicing in this manner, there will be no hindrance.
One who practices correctly is neither bound nor liberated.
Why is this? Because one who possesses correct contemplation has no severance and no pursuit regarding all phenomena.
"If it is thus, this is called right view that perceives all phenomena;
such is right view. What is right view?
It is the non-perception of phenomena."
What is called "view" refers to the unreal discourse of non-arising; one who speaks of the unreal is said to speak the name of non-arising.
"As I have taught, when one first perceives that all phenomena are unarisen through wisdom, and reaches the stage of certainty, it is called right view."
If one perceives in this way, it is called reaching the state of correctness (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
By what causes and conditions is it named the state of correctness?
Both "self" and "non-self" are equal; when all dharmas arise in the same manner as non-self, this is called the state of correctness.
The Scripture on the Collection of All Merit,
Scroll Two: The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Collection of All Merit,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare, World-Honored One!
How rare, Sugata!

Since all dharmas are by nature eternally quiescent in this way, that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is able to hear this Dharma, is able to know this Dharma, and is able to believe this Dharma, yet does not enter parinirvāṇa midway."
The Buddha told Nārāyaṇa:
"Such is the power of a bodhisattva’s skillful means (upāyakauśalya).
If a bodhisattva accomplishes skillful means, they can attain four dharmas in every moment of thought."
What are these four? They are:
great loving-kindness, great compassion, knowing all-knowledge, and the appearance of Buddhas in the world so that the seed of the Dharma is not severed.

By practicing these four dharmas, one knows that the realm of sentient beings is the mark of the true state (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and knows that the nature of all dharmas is eternally quiescent. Having heard this, one understands and gains faith, yet does not enter *nirvāṇa* midway; this is called the dharma of subduing through knowledge, which benefits sentient beings.
Having known this, one sees even to the point of not seeing. Why is this?
Because of not abandoning any sentient beings.
At that time, the Malla Śuddhasthāman addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not fall into fixed determination.”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! This bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not give rise to any views, yet there is no task he does not accomplish.”

“Śrāvakas do not take all sentient beings as their object, nor the lineage of the Buddha, nor the lineage of the Dharma, nor the Mahāyāna; they abandon omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), do not contemplate omniscience, and do not aspire to omniscience, thereby extinguishing conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and entering the stage of a śrāvaka.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, however, take all sentient beings as their object, take the uninterrupted lineage of the Three Jewels as their object, and take the Mahāyāna as their object; they contemplate omniscience but do not contemplate [the preservation of] their own life. Knowing that all phenomena have a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), they do not enter the fixed position (*samyaktvaniyāma*); taking all sentient beings as their object, they sport in the various dhyānas and do not fall into the stage of a śrāvaka.”
“Good son! For this reason, you should know that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is eternally without self and does not fall into the fixed stage.
At that time, the Malla Netrīśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!
How marvelous, Sugata!
The conduct of Bodhisattvas is beyond the reach of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī was seated in the assembly.
The Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Mañjuśrī, the son of the Dharma King, is seated here in this assembly; how is it that he can remain without speaking regarding this Samādhi that Gathers All Merit?
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa, saying: "Good son!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not practice for the sake of merit; a bodhisattva practices enlightenment not for the sake of gain or reputation, not for rebirth in heaven, not for fiefdoms, not for retinues, not for praise, and not for personal pleasure."
Nārāyaṇa said: “Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva!
By what means does one practice for enlightenment?”
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son!

A bodhisattva practices for enlightenment out of compassion for all sentient beings; for the sake of the Dharma; to liberate all sentient beings from suffering; to sever all unreal afflictions; to endure one's own suffering; and because there is nothing [else] to be done, he practices for enlightenment, not begrudging his body or life."

“Contemplating and knowing that it has no master, no ruler, no abode, no marks, no thought, no transformation, no destruction, no shifting transmigration, no invasion, ruin, or harm; that it is valiant and unconquerable, without cognition or understanding, without indolence, without fear, without dread, without alarm, without terror; that it is neither high nor low and free from flattery or crookedness; that it dwells firm and immovable, delighting in stillness and solitude, being the single path and the single destination—abiding in this one path and practicing this one path for the sake of delivering all sentient beings.”
"It is for the sake of such benefits that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice for enlightenment.
He then asked Mañjuśrī,
"In what manner do Bodhisattvas practice for enlightenment?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are without arising and without cessation; they do not practice non-arising and non-cessation, for they have attained ultimate cessation. Having no further birth and nothing to be expressed, the bodhisattva practices enlightenment in this manner."
"Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa!

A bodhisattva knows that the past mind has already ceased and is incapable of functioning; the future mind has not yet arrived and is incapable of functioning; and the present mind does not abide and is incapable of functioning. Without clinging to the minds of the past, future, or present, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva can practice in this way, it is called the cultivation of bodhi."

"Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa! If a bodhisattva knows that giving, awakening, sentient beings, and the Tathāgata are of one and the same non-dual practice; that ethical discipline, awakening, sentient beings, and the Tathāgata are of one and the same non-dual practice; that patience, awakening, sentient beings, and the Tathāgata are of one and the same non-dual practice; that diligence, awakening, sentient beings, and the Tathāgata are of one and the same non-dual practice; that meditative concentration, awakening, sentient beings, and the Tathāgata are of one and the same non-dual practice; and that wisdom, awakening, sentient beings, and the Tathāgata are of one and the same non-dual practice—then when a bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās in this way, they do not destroy or corrupt the nature and characteristics of their practice. It is in this manner that a bodhisattva cultivates awakening."
"Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa!
A bodhisattva contemplates that form is empty and devoid of activity.
Just as one contemplates the emptiness of form;
One contemplates that feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty and without activity.
Form is empty and inexhaustible; form is ultimately exhausted because it is empty.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—the consciousness is empty and inexhaustible; consciousness is ultimately exhausted because it is empty.
Just as their nature is inexhaustible, so all dharmas are inexhaustible;
form is inexhaustible, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are inexhaustible.
If there is a bodhisattva who practices in this manner, this is called cultivating the practice of bodhi.
"Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa!

When a bodhisattva diligently abandons the practices of ordinary beings, yet does not give rise to the practice of Buddha-dharmas, does not produce the practice of saṃsāra, does not fulfill the practice of nirvāṇa, does not perceive the accomplishment of any unwholesome dharmas, and does not accumulate wholesome dharmas nor contemplate them as distinct entities—thus understanding and knowing the nature of indestructible practice—this is the practice of bodhi."
Nārāyaṇa! When a bodhisattva practices in this way, it is called cultivating the practice of awakening.
Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas understand that the realm of sentient beings is immeasurable and the dharma-realm is immeasurable; they practice the inexhaustible cessation of the realms of sentient beings and the dharma-realm. Why is this?
Because the realm of sentient beings and the dharma-realm are non-dual, they have no dual activity and no dual characteristics.
The dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases; the realm of sentient beings neither increases nor decreases.
As is the characteristic of the dharma-realm, so too is the characteristic of the realm of sentient beings.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva understands that all phenomena are signless; thus, they do not exhaust the practice of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), nor do they exhaust the practice of the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*);
they do not exhaust the practice of the realm of phenomena, nor do they increase the practice of the realm of phenomena;
they do not exhaust the practice of the realm of sentient beings, nor do they increase the practice of the realm of sentient beings.
Nor does one dwell in other fetters arising from deluded conceptualization and inversion.

Thus, through correct contemplation, one skillfully understands all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), neither destroying the formations of existence nor destroying the formations of self, sentient beings, or life-span.
"Nārāyaṇa! When a bodhisattva practices in this way, it is called 'cultivating the conduct of enlightenment.

When the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī expounded these various dharmas of conduct, sixteen devaputras who had previously turned toward the Mahāyāna now attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, the Malla Śuddhasthāma, desiring to make offerings and to protect this sutra, spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who believe in and understand this sutra, they shall obtain all manner of goodness, prosperity, and auspiciousness."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Free from Māra said to Mañjuśrī,
“I, too, wish to speak of the conduct of a bodhisattva. Mañjuśrī replied:
“Good son! Now is the very time; you may expound it.
Bodhisattva Free from Māra said:
“Mañjuśrī! To practice all dharmas is the bodhisattva practice; to practice all demonic deeds is the bodhisattva practice; to practice all the deeds of sentient beings is the bodhisattva practice;

to practice the path of those in training (śaikṣa) or the path of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) is the bodhisattva practice; and to practice the path of the pratyekabuddha is the bodhisattva practice.”
"Why is this? Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva should study universally.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa asked the Devaputra Vimukta-māra:
"How does a bodhisattva train in and practice all the conducts of sentient beings?
The devaputra replied, "Nārāyaṇa!"
A bodhisattva should train in eighty-four thousand modes of conduct.
What are these eighty-four thousand modes of conduct?

They are: twenty-one thousand modes of conduct characterized by desire, twenty-one thousand modes of conduct characterized by hatred, twenty-one thousand modes of conduct characterized by delusion, and twenty-one thousand modes of conduct characterized by an equal mixture of these three.

A bodhisattva should fully enter into all these practices: the practice of abandoning and detaching from desire, the practice of abandoning and detaching from hatred, the practice of abandoning and detaching from delusion, and the practice of abandoning and detaching from the equal proportions [of the defilements].

The Bodhisattva practices all the conduct of sentient beings, yet remains unstained by such conduct; he manifests all the various conducts of sentient beings for the sake of transforming them. This is called the Bodhisattva’s practice of the path to enlightenment.
Nārāyaṇa said: "O Son of Heaven!
In what way are all the practices of Māra the practices of a bodhisattva?"
The devaputra said:

“All demonic activities enter the mind of a bodhisattva; the bodhisattva should awaken to them as they arise and not follow them, remaining unbound by demonic conduct. Entering into all such practices, he should cultivate them so as to show the devas of Māra no opportunity for interference, and he should transform the māras so that they abandon their demonic deeds.”
Nārāyaṇa said: "O Son of Heaven!
How is it that training in the practices of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas constitutes the practice of a bodhisattva?"
The devaputra said: "Good son!

All such conditioned activities (saṃskāra) are activities of true nature, activities without retribution, activities without abiding, activities without destination, and activities without arising; they are to be understood as self-acting."
“A bodhisattva should practice in this manner.
Having spoken thus, the devaputra Vimukta addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī:
“O son of good family!
"You should now further explain such a practice. Mañjuśrī said,
"O Devaputra!"
The conduct of a bodhisattva transcends all realms.

Why is this? This conduct does not fall within the category of the realm of the eye, nor does it fall within the categories of the realms of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena (*dharma*).
"O Son of Heaven!
Therefore, you should know that the various practices undertaken by this virtuous man transcend all realms.
Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!"
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices in this manner, they are approved by all Buddhas and are free from fault.
To practice in such a way is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the correct path.
The devaputra said:
"Mañjuśrī! How does a bodhisattva practice that which is permitted by all Buddhas as being worthy of performance?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra!
The ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) of all phenomena is inherently empty; it is in this way that the Tathāgata awakens to and knows it."
If a bodhisattva dwells in such practice of the Dharma as is approved by the Buddhas,
yet gives rise to views and attachments regarding even nirvāṇa, they then deceive all the Buddhas.
“Son of Heaven!
The ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all phenomena is signless (*animitta*); it is thus that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has awakened to them.
If there is a bodhisattva who constructs signs for phenomena and dwells together with those signs, he deceives all Buddhas.”

All dharmas are the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and are wishless (*apraṇihita*); the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has awakened to them as such: they are without activity, without reality, without birth, without arising, without existence, without form, without marks, yet not without marks; they neither come nor go, nor do they abide; their intrinsic nature is pure, their intrinsic nature is luminous, and their nature is eternally extinguished. All dharmas are like empty space, and the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has awakened to them as such.
If a bodhisattva were to obtain even the slightest [grasping] regarding the nature of these dharmas, he would be deceiving the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
“Devaputra! If this bodhisattva dwells together with emptiness and gives rise to attachment through views;
if this bodhisattva dwells together with signlessness and gives rise to attachment through views;”
If a bodhisattva dwells together with the wishless while giving rise to views and attachments, they deceive all the Buddhas.

If a bodhisattva transcends the three realms and knows that all phenomena are without reality, without birth, without arising, without existence, without form, without marks, without coming, without going, and without abiding; that their fundamental nature is pure, their fundamental nature is luminous, and their fundamental nature is eternally extinguished—being identical to space and fundamentally stainless; [then they do not deceive the Buddhas].
"If one knows in this way, this is called a bodhisattva not deceiving the Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Mañjuśrī:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Mañjuśrī! You have spoken these words well.
If a bodhisattva practices in this manner, it is called the practice of awakening (bodhicaryā), and they will swiftly receive the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).
“Mañjuśrī! In the past, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I did not receive any prediction regarding the various practices in which I resided. Why is this?

I had practices characterized by signs, practices with dependence, and practices with attachment; later, upon seeing the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I transcended all such practices. From the very first moment I saw him, I became free from the view of all practices and realized that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-arising.
At that time, Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed upon me this prediction, saying:
"After this, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"At that time, I attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Therefore, Mañjuśrī,
if there is a bodhisattva who wishes to swiftly attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, they should practice in this chapter in this manner, remaining unattached to all dharmas."
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by taking what dharma as a condition does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attain the patience of non-arising?”
The Buddha said, “Mañjuśrī!

One attains the patience of non-arising by taking the aggregates, elements, and sense bases as conditions; one attains the patience regarding all dharmas. Furthermore, one attains the patience of dharmas by taking permanence, bliss, self, and purity as conditions.”
Mañjuśrī! That which is called "patience" (kṣānti) is named the inexhaustibility of all dharmas as their object;
that which is called "patience" is termed "correctness."
Mañjuśrī! The objective referent of patience does not function in conjunction with worldly dharmas;

it does not function in conjunction with the dharmas of ordinary persons, nor with the dharmas of those in training, nor with the dharmas of those beyond training, nor with the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, nor with the dharmas of bodhisattvas, nor with the dharmas of buddhas.
Not functioning in conjunction with any phenomena is called the attainment of patience (*kṣānti*).
Abandoning all conceptual attachments to phenomena is termed patience.

This patience does not reside within the categories of eye and form, ear and sound, nose and fragrance, tongue and taste, body and touch, or mind and mental objects; being neither exhausted nor inexhaustible, it is termed patience.
"This patience, moreover, does not depart from this realm; this is what is called patience.

When these words on patience were spoken, five hundred bodhisattvas who had previously planted roots of goodness under former buddhas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and spoke thus:
"This Samādhi of the Accumulation of All Merit enables us to abide in that which we abide in, and it also causes us to fulfill immeasurable dharmas."
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should listen with a sincere mind to all profound dharmas and should cultivate and accumulate them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa asked Mañjuśrī:
"How does a bodhisattva accomplish what is to be done regarding this profound Dharma? Mañjuśrī replied,
"If a bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are neither created nor uncreated, this is called a bodhisattva who has accomplished what is to be done."

If, having realized that all phenomena are devoid of activity, one neither clings to them, does not create them, nor forgets them, this is called a bodhisattva who has accomplished what was to be done.
If such a bodhisattva remains without expectation of gratitude for whatever they have done, this is called knowing gratitude.
Conditioned and unconditioned phenomena do not give rise to high or low; one neither attains an agent nor that which is acted upon—namely, performing acts of giving while abiding in dedication.
Furthermore, one does not attain giving, does not attain awakening, and does not attain self or other; this is called the bodhisattva who has completed what was to be done.

Guarding the pure precepts and dedicating them toward Bodhi, yet not apprehending the precepts; likewise practicing, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, yet not apprehending wisdom—this is called the bodhisattva who has completed what was to be done.
If one does not perceive the wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind, one should know that this bodhisattva has already accomplished what was to be done;
if one does not perceive the physical form, nor the adornments accumulated by speech and mind, one should know that this bodhisattva has already accomplished what was to be done.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Constant Diligence said to Mañjuśrī, "I,
too, wish to speak of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have already accomplished what was to be done."
Mañjuśrī said: "Good son!
Now is precisely the right time; you may speak."
The Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent said to Mañjuśrī,
“If a bodhisattva can cause even a single sentient being to enter into the Buddha-dharma, that bodhisattva has accomplished what was to be done.”

If a bodhisattva receives food from sentient beings and gives it to others, not out of fear but with the intention that all may be gathered within unsurpassed enlightenment, this is called the purity of the bodhisattva’s field of merit.
If both the donor and the recipient act in accordance with the Dharma, this is called the Bodhisattva’s purity of both parties.

If a Bodhisattva causes others to hear through the voice of the Buddha, while personally abiding in generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, maintaining right mindfulness; and if, within the great assembly, they preach the six *pāramitās* so that others may hear, remember, and uphold such roots of goodness—then one should know that this Bodhisattva has accomplished what was to be done and is capable of digesting offerings.

"If a bodhisattva practices patience, even when reviled and insulted by enemies, bandits, outcasts, and the like, they feel neither anger nor resentment; rather, for the sake of causing these sentient beings to give rise to faith and joy, they diligently cultivate vigor and abide in the power of vigor—know that this bodhisattva has already accomplished what was to be done."

"If a bodhisattva, even though the four continents were filled with genuine gold and jewels, would not greedily covet those treasures and thus speak falsely; and if, when asked about the Dharma by others, they do not speak of what is not the Dharma out of partiality—know that this bodhisattva has already accomplished what was to be done."
"If there is a bodhisattva who has gone without food for seven days, and someone comes and says to him:
'If you can renounce the mind of enlightenment and kill living beings, I shall give you food.'"
Yet this bodhisattva would never do so, for he knows that this bodhisattva has already accomplished what was to be done.

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva sees sharp blades and fierce fires filling the entire world, he should pass through them to go and listen to the Dharma; he does not cherish his own body or life, training himself in this way: "

"Recollection of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements is easy to obtain; however, a Buddha is difficult to encounter, the Dharma is difficult to hear, and sentient beings who revere the Dharma are exceedingly rare.
Having formed this thought, he enters the assembly to listen to the Dharma, knowing that this bodhisattva has already accomplished what was to be done.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If a bodhisattva hears from another a single four-line verse concerning either ethical discipline or generosity, and gives rise to joy in their heart, this is superior to attaining the rank of a great wheel-turning monarch;
if one causes even a single person to hear such a verse, it is superior to attaining the station of Śakra or Brahmā."
One knows that this bodhisattva has accomplished what was to be done.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, if a bodhisattva is able to dwell among the assembly and gives rise to great joy in their extensive learning, directing that extensive learning toward omniscience; and if they do not experience such great delight at obtaining treasures filling the trichiliocosm as they do when dedicating their own roots of goodness toward the Buddha-way for the sake of a single sentient being, taking this as their celebration—one knows that this bodhisattva has accomplished what was to be done.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

For the sake of transforming all sentient beings, a bodhisattva should apply diligent effort, firmly adorn themselves, cultivate and accumulate extensive learning, and sacrifice their own limbs and members; yet their mind remains unchanged by the eight worldly dharmas.
If such a bodhisattva is for the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom, they would rather sacrifice their body and life than abandon their observance of the precepts."
A bodhisattva should practice patience, being able to endure all evil and unwholesome sounds;
a bodhisattva should apply diligent effort to adorn the buddha-fields; a bodhisattva should dwell alone in a secluded place in order not to lose the path to enlightenment;
and a bodhisattva should not lose right mindfulness in order to cultivate and accumulate the six pāramitās.
“A bodhisattva should be without attachment, diligently fulfilling the precepts and performing virtuous deeds so as not to abandon any sentient beings.
A bodhisattva should adorn themselves with firm vows for the sake of the seeds of the Buddha-dharma.”
A bodhisattva should distance themselves from all flattery and hypocrisy, because their physical, verbal, and mental conduct must be fundamentally honest and upright.
A bodhisattva should purify their own aspirations and intentions, for the sake of rescuing and providing refuge to all sentient beings.
A bodhisattva should practice without mental constructions, because they do not cling to body or life.
A bodhisattva should speak with sweetness, gentleness, and kindness, because they skillfully come to offer greetings.
A bodhisattva should always be the first to speak with kindness, for they are free from anger and resentment that would prevent them from speaking.
A bodhisattva should be like the earth, for they are free from love and hatred.
A bodhisattva should be gentle, mild, and pliant, because they share a heart of joy with others.
A bodhisattva should be easy to instruct, because they swiftly receive the teachings.
A bodhisattva should eliminate arrogance and remain humble before all sentient beings.
A bodhisattva should be like a dog, for they do not deceive any sentient beings and do not violate their original vows.
A bodhisattva should give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings, because all things are empty.
A bodhisattva should give rise to great compassion among all sentient beings for the sake of accomplishing their great benefit.
A bodhisattva should give rise to great joy because of delighting in the cultivation and accumulation of all roots of goodness.
A bodhisattva should practice great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*), because they do not regard any of the pleasures of the five desires.
A bodhisattva should be free from greed and stinginess, even to the point of relinquishing their own body.
A bodhisattva should not be attached to "mine," because they do not crave any material wealth.
A bodhisattva should cultivate a mind of great renunciation, because they relinquish all conceptual constructions.
“A bodhisattva should be fully endowed with great wealth, by means of the seven noble riches.
A bodhisattva should be firm and steadfast in resolve, for the sake of consolidating all roots of goodness.”
A bodhisattva should never be satisfied, because they must cultivate and accumulate the immeasurable merits of a Buddha.
A bodhisattva should be courageous and strong in wisdom, because they must vanquish the four māras.
A bodhisattva should act as a great king of physicians, for they skillfully treat all diseases of the afflictions.
A bodhisattva should act as one worthy of offerings, for they do not abandon the bodhicitta.
A bodhisattva should act as a field of merit in order to provide illumination for all sentient beings.
A bodhisattva should be like a lotus flower, for they are not defiled by the mud of the world.
A bodhisattva should be like a boat or raft, for the purpose of ferrying all sentient beings across.
A bodhisattva should be like a bridge, for they harbor no discriminatory thoughts toward sentient beings of superior, middling, or inferior capacities.
A bodhisattva should be like a great pond, for they are single-mindedly devoted to the water of the True Dharma, which is inexhaustible.
A bodhisattva should be like the great ocean, for they never tire of their constant pursuit of extensive learning.
A bodhisattva should be like a great mountain, for they cannot be shaken.
A bodhisattva should be well-established and firm, like a door-sill.
A bodhisattva should be free from attachment to all possessions and material wealth.
A bodhisattva should bring the mind under control so as not to regress.
A bodhisattva should be like a great king because of their supreme excellence.
A bodhisattva should be like Śakra, because they are honored and esteemed by all sentient beings.
A bodhisattva should be like Brahmā, for he is a sovereign Dharma King.
A bodhisattva should bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, leading them to ultimate peace and happiness in nirvana.
"A bodhisattva should act as a parent to sentient beings for the sake of providing them with clothing and benefits.
A bodhisattva should remain unharmed regarding all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas."
A bodhisattva should be free from causing harm, because their mind is impartial toward both those who are kin and those who are not.
A bodhisattva should neither form attachments nor place blind trust, because they have fully understood the nature of all sense bases (*āyatana*) that arise.
A bodhisattva should be a master of the gift of Dharma, because they relinquish everything.
A bodhisattva should remain free from all negligence and indolence, because they seek to accumulate the requisites for awakening.

Mañjuśrī! A bodhisattva should always be firm and vigorous in their diligence, cultivating and accumulating all precepts and virtuous conduct for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Constant Diligence:
“Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!”
He has well explained the perceptions regarding how one should abide in all conditioned phenomena. Good son!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to attain this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit, he should diligently cultivate all merit and must not abandon any merit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are those who attain this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit, they shall not fall into the evil realms nor be born within the eight difficulties; they shall sever all poverty, their minds will always be autonomous, their faculties will be complete, and they will be well-adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.”
"They have attained great eloquence and inexhaustible dharmas; they have attained dharanis and non-forgetfulness of mindfulness, so as to give rise to all merit and turn the wheel of Dharma.
They have attained the stage of consecration, being honored by Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, and all sentient beings."
"They have attained the full range of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), because they penetrate the death here and birth there of all beings.
They have attained great mastery (*vaśitā*), because they enter into every place of rebirth wherever they may be born.
They have attained a great fief (*mahāviṣaya*), because they cause all dharmas to increase."
One attains the light of wisdom because one is free from evil and false views.
One attains great renown because of all the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
One attains great subduing because of all persons who are śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
They skillfully discern the various faculties for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
They possess mastery of supernormal powers through the gates of the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis.
They attain non-conceptual giving through their understanding of the nature of giving.
They attain the precept of non-abiding because the three types of precepts are pure;
they possess immeasurable patience because their heart of loving-kindness pervades all sentient beings;
and they practice diligence because their minds are free from weariness.
He attains the perfection of dhyāna and understands tranquility in order to transform sentient beings born into the desire realm;
he is adorned with pure wisdom because he skillfully observes sounds and voices.
This is called the "Pure Eye," for it is able to see the Path.

It is never apart from seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma; it is not separate from emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). It is able to uphold all the teachings of all Buddhas and never ceases to behold them. It attains the community of non-regressive Bodhisattvas because it has removed all obstacles to the merits of all Buddha-fields, because it has subdued all Māras and triumphed over the four Māras, and because it has attained the profound Dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*) of the non-regressive Dharma.

They are able to swiftly penetrate and fulfill the Buddha-dharma; teachings never before heard spontaneously enter their ears; because they desire and vow to fully acquire all the merits of all buddha-fields, they attain peace and security, being free from all habitual tendencies.
"They have attained a body of mastery, manifesting universally throughout the three realms.

They cannot be subdued by any non-Buddhists; they skillfully guard the Dharma, having sacrificed their own bodies and lives in the presence of the Buddhas to protect the True Dharma; and though they behold the realm of the Buddhas, they do not ultimately enter parinirvāṇa."
"He has attained fearlessness because he is without fear among the assembly; whatever he does is preceded by wisdom because his mind is free from worldly concerns.
He manifests great adornment through supernatural transformations; he attains great power because he transcends all harm;
his pure voice resounds, being heard throughout all worlds."
Their minds are great and courageous, for they crush and subdue all the armies of Māra;
they have reached the further shore of supernormal powers, for they can shake all Buddha-worlds;
they have attained great eloquence, for their mastery of dharma, phrasing, and meaning is unimpeded and unhindered.
With unimpeded understanding and without negligence, he dwells performing the Buddha-work to manifest all-knowledge to all sentient beings. "Nārāyaṇa!
If a bodhisattva enters this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit, he attains such immeasurable merit through these signs, characteristics, and manifestations."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
May all sentient beings attain the Samādhi of the Accumulation of All Merit and Virtue just as this.”
Whatever merits the Bodhisattva attains through this samādhi, he causes all sentient beings to attain those same merits—merits that are not possessed by any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
"Bhagavān!
If there are bodhisattvas who do not get to hear this treasure of samādhi, or who do not understand it even after hearing it, you should know that such persons are possessed by Māra."
The Buddha said,
“Nārāyaṇa! So it is, so it is!”
It is as you have said.

If there are bodhisattvas who hear of the merit produced by this samādhi—whether it has already been produced, is being produced now, or will be produced in the future—it shall be immeasurable and boundless.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa asked Mañjuśrī:
"If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to cultivate and practice this samādhi, what dharmas should they practice?"

Mañjuśrī said: "A bodhisattva who wishes to attain this samādhi does not abandon the dharmas of ordinary beings as a means of upholding the Buddha-dharma; practicing in this way, they are neither associated with dharma nor associated with non-dharma.
Practicing in this way, although they circulate through birth and death, they do not study the dharmas of birth and death, nor are they defiled by birth and death."
Although they study *nirvāṇa*, they do not enter the *nirvāṇa* of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa!

If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to study this samādhi, they should further increase and accumulate all merit and virtue (*puṇya*). They should not give rise to conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding any conditioned or unconditioned merits, whether tainted or untainted; nor should they give rise to discrimination between the wholesome and the unwholesome, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the mundane and the supramundane, or sin and merit. They should understand that all merit and virtue enter into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)."

"Whether it be the practice of meritorious dharmas, the practice of sinful dharmas, or the practice of indeterminate dharmas, all enter into the dharma-nature; one should thus perceive that the merit and so forth of sentient beings arise from what is unreal."
The merit of these sentient beings and the merit of the Buddha are entirely equal; no distinction is seen, for the dharma-realm is without difference and arises without differentiation.

Whether it be the merit of ordinary beings, the merit of those in training (*śaikṣa*), the merit of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the merit of pratyekabuddhas, the merit of bodhisattvas, or the merit of the Perfectly Awakened One—all are unreal because they lack substantiality. They have no location, nor do they lack a location. One should know and understand that the nature of merit is such that all sentient beings are equal.
“Good son! Just as all forms depend upon the four great elements, so too is the merit of a bodhisattva.
It pervades all places, yet never gives rise to the arrogance or negligence of merit; one should know it to be a phenomenon subject to impermanence, exhaustion, and cessation.”
"Nārāyaṇa! If a bodhisattva wishes to attain this samādhi, they shall not be startled or terrified by four things.
What are these four?

Nārāyaṇa! His great compassion for all sentient beings is boundless; his buddha-fields are boundless; his buddha-wisdom is boundless; and his entry into the mental activities of all sentient beings is boundless.
A bodhisattva should not give rise to fear regarding these four infinitudes.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should understand and know the four inconceivables.
What are the four?

Karma and its retribution are inconceivable; the various and manifold differences in the diverse conducts of all sentient beings are inconceivable; the conduct of the Buddha-Tathāgatas is inconceivable; and the arising of the various pure practices of Bodhisattvas is inconceivable.
"Nārāyaṇa! These are called the four inconceivable things, which you should understand and know. Good son!"
The Bodhisattva understands and attains four kinds of inexhaustibility.
What are these four?
Inexhaustibility of merit, inexhaustibility of fulfilling vows, inexhaustibility of eloquence, and inexhaustibility of ultimate wisdom.
Nārāyaṇa! This is how a bodhisattva attains the four inexhaustibles. Nārāyaṇa!
A bodhisattva should practice four dharmas.
What are these four? They are:

never being satisfied with the adornment of roots of goodness; never being satisfied with the dedication of skillful means toward all that is inexhaustible; and never being satisfied with taking up the various adornments of all buddha-fields to adorn one's own buddha-field. (In the Sanskrit original, one item is missing.)
"Nārāyaṇa! A bodhisattva should thus cultivate and practice these four dharmas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa again asked Mañjuśrī:
"To whose hands shall this *Sarvapuṇyasamuccaya-samādhi-sūtra* come?
Whether it reaches the dwellings of bodhisattvas, or those who practice dhyāna, or those who practice patience, or those who live as householders, or those who have gone forth?"
Mañjuśrī said: "Nārāyaṇa!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears of this samādhi—whether it reaches their ears, their hands, or their home—and that person does not give rise to slander, such a person I do not call a householder; I shall call such a person one who has gone forth."
Why is this? It is because this bodhisattva diligently cultivates the discernment of this samādhi.
Such a person shall be able to eliminate all conceptualizations, and in every dwelling place, all their merit and wisdom will be inexhaustible and undispersed.
"Nārāyaṇa! For the sake of transforming all sentient beings, bodhisattvas manifest various forms, colors, and appearances. Nārāyaṇa!"
This person reaches all places, just as the sun and moon illuminate the four continents so that everything is clearly revealed.
In this same way, Nārāyaṇa,
it is with the Bodhisattva.

Not relying on any difficulties, although dwelling at home, he does not rely on the household; nor is he one who has left the home-life, for he does not rely on the dharma of a śramaṇa. He cannot be described as either of these two.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva does not rely on anything that exists, nor upon the sense bases (*āyatana*). "Nārāyaṇa!..."
Just as a vessel made of lapis lazuli does not lose its essential nature regardless of where it is placed, so it is, Nārāyaṇa!

If there is a bodhisattva who dwells in this samādhi, even if they live at home, one should say of that person that they have gone forth; they are able not to lose the essential nature of this dharma-realm.
At that time, Nārāyaṇa asked Mañjuśrī,
“In what state does a bodhisattva mahāsattva abide so as to be able to not lose this Samādhi of Gathering All Merit, and thereby attain such adornment of inexhaustible merit and wisdom?”
Mañjuśrī said: “Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have four abodes.
What are the four?

What is meant by this? It is that a bodhisattva does not dwell upon body, life, or various gains and offerings; they dwell in the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; they do not dwell in the fixed positions of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; and while aspiring for the Buddha’s wisdom and unimpeded eloquence, they are free from arrogance, false conceptualization, and discrimination, nor do they cling to such states of dwelling.
This bodhisattva dwells in the liberation of all sentient beings, yet does not dwell in the notions of self, person, sentient being, life-span, or individual. "Nārāyaṇa!
These are the four abodes of a bodhisattva:

the adornment of the most supreme abode is inexhaustible; the adornment of the great mass of merit is inexhaustible; the great mass of wisdom severs all views; and the fulfillment and perfection of the arising of all Buddha-dharmas.
Nārāyaṇa asked Mañjuśrī,
“How does a bodhisattva attain this state of dwelling and thereby receive the name ‘one who has gone forth’? Mañjuśrī replied:

“Nārāyaṇa! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains this dwelling place: namely, dwelling in loving-kindness, dwelling in compassion, dwelling in sympathetic joy, and dwelling in equanimity. Nārāyaṇa!”
This is for a bodhisattva to dwell in the four abodes. "Nārāyaṇa!
Whether a bodhisattva dwells in a village or town, or dwells in a secluded place, if they dwell in these four abodes of the brahma-vihāras, it is called dwelling in the correct abode."
If one departs from these four abodes of the Brahma-conduct, even if one dwells within a proper palace, hall, or pavilion, it cannot be called an "abode.
Nārāyaṇa! Such a person is said to deceive all humans, devas, and asuras, and to consume offerings in vain.
"Nārāyaṇa! If a bodhisattva abides in any other forms of pure conduct (brahmacarya), they are all subsumed within these four pure conducts. Why is this?
Nārāyaṇa! This dwelling place of the Brahma-faring is extremely difficult to attain.
If there are those who do not see these four Brahma-farings as the conditions for noble dhyāna, they possess the view of a self in this world and have not severed their conceit.
Nārāyaṇa said: “Mañjuśrī!
How does a bodhisattva come to be named as one who dwells in this loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity?”
Mañjuśrī said: "Nārāyaṇa! If there is a bodhisattva who forms such a thought as this:"
"I shall deliver all sentient beings"—
this is called abiding in loving-kindness;
"I shall liberate all sentient beings."
"This is called abiding in compassion;
'I must cause all sentient beings to abide in the Buddha-dharma'—
this is called abiding in joy."
"I shall bring all sentient beings to tranquility by means of supramundane dharmas.
This is called abiding in equanimity.
"Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa!"
If a bodhisattva understands that all dharma-realms are empty, this is called abiding in loving-kindness;
if a bodhisattva understands that all dharma-realms are quiescent, this is called abiding in compassion;
if a bodhisattva understands that all dharma-realms are without attachment, without bondage, and without liberation, this is called abiding in sympathetic joy.
