If a bodhisattva understands that the entire dharma-realm neither goes nor comes, this is called abiding in equanimity (upekṣā).
Nārāyaṇa! This is called a bodhisattva abiding in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
"Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa!
If a bodhisattva sees the dharma of non-self and is not startled or afraid, this is called abiding in loving-kindness;
if they see all sentient beings as quiescent and are not startled or afraid, this is called abiding in compassion."
If, upon hearing that all Buddha-dharmas are equal and identical to a single Buddha-dharma, one is not startled or afraid, this is called abiding in joy;
if, upon hearing that all lands are inexhaustible, one is not startled or afraid, this is called abiding in equanimity.
"Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa!

That which is free from all obstructions and hindrances is called loving-kindness (*maitrī*); that which rescues sentient beings from suffering is called compassion (*karuṇā*); that which is entirely free from affliction is called sympathetic joy (*muditā*); and that which is neither elevated nor depressed is called equanimity (*upekṣā*)."
"Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa!
There is compassion, but it is not great loving-kindness and great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*).
Great loving-kindness and great compassion are not possessed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas."
The compassion of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings; this is called compassion, but not great compassion.
What, then, is called great kindness and great compassion?

If one gives rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings and delivers them from their suffering and affliction, this is called the bodhisattva’s great kindness and great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*).
If one is born within the five destinies, for the sake of all sentient beings one personally relinquishes one's own happiness and forms this thought:
"These sentient beings have fallen into wrong paths; I shall establish them so that they abide in the right path."
"This is called the great loving-kindness and great compassion of a bodhisattva. Nārāyaṇa!
Therefore, you should know that while śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess loving-kindness and compassion, they do not possess great loving-kindness and great compassion."
"Nārāyaṇa! For this reason, a bodhisattva should cultivate and fulfill great loving-kindness and great compassion.
When this Dharma of great loving-kindness and great compassion was being taught, eight thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and spoke these words:
"We, too, shall abide in the great loving-kindness and great compassion as taught by Mañjuśrī.
Thereupon, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the samādhi of "Gathering All Merit," and eight thousand sentient beings were freed from dust and defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, World-Honored One, is named for the marks of a hundred merits; by what causes and conditions has he obtained such marks?"
The Buddha told Nārāyaṇa:

"If all sentient beings in worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, were each to become a universal wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin rāja), the aggregate of merit and virtue of them all would equal the merit and virtue possessed by a single Śakra."

In as many worlds as there are sands in the Ganges throughout the ten directions, all sentient beings may achieve a mass of merit equal to that of Śakra; yet the entire mass of merit possessed by all those Śakras is equal to the mass of merit possessed by a single Brahmā King.

"Nārāyaṇa! If all sentient beings in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were to achieve a mass of merit equal to that of a Brahmā King, the total mass of merit possessed by all those Brahmā Kings would be equal to the mass of merit possessed by a single Śrāvaka."

"Nārāyaṇa! If all sentient beings throughout as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were to become śrāvakas, the total accumulation of their merit would equal the merit possessed by a single pratyekabuddha."
"Nārāyaṇa! Suppose all sentient beings in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were each to fully accomplish the accumulation of virtues of a pratyekabuddha. Nārāyaṇa!"

If all the accumulations of merit belonging to all these śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas were combined into one, it would equal the merit of a single bodhisattva who has accomplished this Samādhi of the Accumulation of All Merits; yet even that accumulation of merit would still fall short of the merit of the [bodhisattva] who possesses such qualities.
"Nārāyaṇa! The merit and roots of goodness accomplished by this bodhisattva are immeasurable and boundless. Nārāyaṇa!"

If all sentient beings throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions were each to attain the mass of merit from this "Samādhi of Gathering All Merit," and if that collection of virtues were multiplied a hundred thousand times over, it would still not equal the merit of a single mark of a Buddha;
this is called the Tathāgata’s mark of a hundred merits. No sentient being is able to fathom it; therefore, the Tathāgata’s marks of a hundred merits are called inconceivable.

When this Dharma discourse on the marks of the hundred merits was being spoken, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, a great light shone everywhere, hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, and the heavens rained down exquisite flowers.

All the devas, humans, asuras, and others in the world marveled at this unprecedented event; they cried out "Excellent! with loud voices, prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, and paid homage at the feet of the World-Honored One, saying these words:

"If there are sentient beings who resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path of enlightenment, they will swiftly obtain great and virtuous benefit, for they shall attain a body adorned with such marks of a hundred merits, surpassing all the accumulated virtues of Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas."
Any sentient beings who hear this Jewel Samādhi that Gathers All Merit will obtain great benefit.
Having heard it, they should practice according to what has been taught.
"Bhagavān!
In whatever land this sutra exists, you should know that therein the good sons and good daughters are sustained by the power of the Buddha and are able to circulate this sutra."
“World-Honored One!
Even if the world were filled with a great conflagration, I would pass through it to go and hear this sutra.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is! Good son, it is just as you have said."
If there are good men or good women who do not hear this sutra, you should know that such persons are possessed by Māra. Good man!
If a bodhisattva hears this Samādhi Sutra and is unable to receive and uphold it, I do not say that they have truly heard it.

"If one hears [the Dharma] but does not uphold it, does not read it, does not recite it, does not propagate it, and does not extensively analyze and explain it to the great assembly, this is not called 'much learning.
At that time, the great assembly all spoke with one voice, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“I pray that you will protect this sutra titled ‘The Samādhi of the Collection of All Merit’ and cause it to spread widely.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from the mark of the white tuft between his brows, which illuminated immeasurable and boundless worlds.
From within this radiance, such a voice issued forth:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has already protected this sutra.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda! The Tathāgata will not remain long; in three months’ time, he shall enter parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder. Ānanda!”
I now entrust this sūtra of samādhi to you; receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it in detail. Ānanda!
If there are sentient beings who uphold this sūtra, for those individuals, the Buddha has not entered parinirvāṇa, nor has the Dharma ceased to exist.
Why is this? Ānanda!
If there is anyone who reveals and expounds this sutra, you should know that such a person is seeing the Buddha.
"If one distinguishes, expounds, and elucidates the words and meanings within the great assembly, it should be known that such a person is a guardian of the True Dharma.
At that time, Ānanda wept with tears streaming down his face and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"

May you remain for one eon, or remain for a hundred eons, or remain for a thousand eons, bringing peace and security to many, providing great benefit, and bringing profit, peace, and security to humans and devas.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Do not weep in sorrow. If you receive, uphold, read, recite, and cause this sutra to be widely circulated so that it is not lost or forgotten, for as long as you do so, you shall always behold the Buddha."
Why is this? The Buddha-Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the physical body, cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks, and cannot be seen by means of the secondary characteristics.
"Ānanda! If there are those who obtain the sight of such sūtras as these, they shall be regarded as seeing the Buddha.

When this sūtra had been spoken, Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince, Nārāyaṇa Bodhisattva, the Malla Śuddhasthāman, the great assembly of bodhisattvas, the venerable Ānanda and the great multitude of śrāvakas, along with all humans, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and the people of the world, having heard what the Buddha had taught, were all greatly filled with joy.
The Scripture on the Accumulation of All Merit, Scroll II.
